CHAPTER 1 - THE BASICS

A FEW WORDS

Fantasy roleplaying is a captivating force that spreads like wildfire, impossible to contain once it touches your soul. My personal journey commenced in 1986 when my older brother brought home those iconic red and blue box sets of a popular roleplaying game. Having been immersed in fantasy game books for years, it was only natural to take the next step.

Under my brother's guidance, I delved into a realm of mythical wonders, where the boundaries were dictated by my imagination and the roll of those beautifully crafted dice. After hours of playing a 1st level Cleric, chosen for my high Wisdom score, I pondered the endless possibilities of this game.

A few days later, I sought out my local gaming shop (a stamp and coin shop near the seafront) and acquired my very first set of dice. It took weeks to save up for that shiny red box, but once I possessed it, my true adventure began—for me and the countless others who would partake in my games throughout the years.

I like to believe that my roleplaying campaigns have left lasting memories on those who have journeyed alongside me. Together, we have unravelled fantasy worlds, challenging gods and battling goblins (as well as the odd tavern brawl). We have traversed the fabric of reality, venturing into dreamscapes and parallel universes. Timelines have fractured, alternate realities have spawned, and great demons have been vanquished at the nexus of time. We have traversed the galaxy in mighty starships (and crashed hover planes into buildings). Formidable supervillains have crumbled before our powers, while tyrants have risen, leaving a legacy of terror upon unfamiliar worlds.

Then there are the moments of pure comedy—the player who crafted a new character just before a momentous battle, only to perish so swiftly that their name went unknown to the party. The psychotic, sociopathic android who consistently led their comrades into blatant death-traps. The bumbling Northman who habitually sprung every trap by opening doors before the rogue could intervene. The chaotic gnome wizard who leaped off a cliff, only to remember he hadn't prepared a feather fall spell—countless tales that continue to bring laughter and merriment.

When reminiscing with past and present players, we fondly recall characters and situations as if they were real occurrences. It both amuses and warms my heart to recall the memories of these remarkable characters. Characters like Parx Tainlel, a priest of the goddess of magic, possessed by a demon and eventually wrested back under the player's control after two decades. Graydon Tainlel, the son of Parx, born of a mortal mother and demon father. These, along with countless others, have inhabited my games for the past 25 years.

This brings me to the book you now hold in your hands. As an experienced Gamesmaster, I have always found the need to house rule and adapt game systems to suit the needs of my players and myself. With the release of the 5th edition of a popular D20 game, I felt that the overarching needs of my gamers had not been fully met. It was then that my younger brother suggested I write my own game, and that seed firmly planted itself in my mind.

On March 5th, 2015, I sat before my computer and began penning the first words of the rulebook now in your possession. Within a month, I conducted alpha playtests, and the work continued with fervour. Read, play, and play again. Hopefully, you will find minimal need to alter the rules to suit your preferences, but if necessary, feel free to share your modifications with me.

Most importantly, have fun……..

Graham Seeney

After over a year of playing the full release of TRG, it became clear that a d20 system was necessary. This new approach begins with TRG: Prime, a streamlined d20 adaptation of the core TRG rules. Skills remain in the same format, but notable changes have been made to critical tables, spells, energy types, and feats.

This adaptation responds to player feedback seeking a more familiar experience. By embracing the d20 framework, TRG: Prime preserves the depth of the original while improving accessibility and pacing, making it an ideal entry point for new players and a fresh challenge for veterans alike.

Gregan Tainlel, the master thief of the Duchy of Aequus, stood hidden in the shadows of the ancient temple of Malkurath, the God of Death. The past few months had been a whirlwind of cunning schemes and narrow escapes, all leading to this moment. The legendary Dark Idol, a relic said to hold the very essence of Malkurath’s power, was within his reach. Tales of its cursed magic, capable of summoning death itself, only made the prize more enticing for a man like Gregan, who thrived on the thrill of impossible odds.

He paused, fingers tracing the scar on his cheek—a reminder of his narrow escape from the catacombs beneath the Imperial Palace of Aequus. The flickering torchlight from the temple’s braziers cast long, skeletal shadows across the stone walls, making the carvings of skulls and serpents seem almost alive. As he crouched behind a cracked pillar, Gregan couldn’t help but reflect on his journey. He had outwitted the city guard, slipped through the grasp of rival thieves, and now stood on the precipice of one of the greatest heists the Numari Empire had ever seen.

The temple’s inner sanctum loomed before him, a massive chamber draped in black silk and filled with the scent of burning incense. At its heart stood the altar of Malkurath, and atop it, the idol—its surface polished to a mirror-like sheen that seemed to absorb the light around it. Gregan’s sharp eyes scanned the room. He knew the priests would have laid traps, and he wouldn’t get a second chance if he mis stepped. The idol was guarded not only by ancient wards of soul magic but also by the vigilant Scythes, the deadly clerics of Malkurath, sworn to protect the relics of their god.

Gregan had prepared for this moment. He recalled the arcane symbols he had deciphered in the forbidden texts stolen from the archives of the Imperial University—a warning of the soul-binding magic that would guard the relic. He pulled a small pouch from his belt and sprinkled a fine, shimmering powder over the ground—a rare alchemical concoction designed to disrupt magical wards. He felt the faint hum of energy dissipate, the oppressive air in the chamber easing slightly.

Just as he stepped towards the altar, a low chant echoed from the far side of the room. Three Scythes entered, clad in robes as dark as the void, their faces obscured by bone-white masks. Leading them was the High Scythe herself, carrying a staff crowned with a sickly green crystal that pulsed with necrotic energy. Gregan’s heart skipped a beat; he had expected guards, but not the temple’s high priestess.

For a fleeting moment, he considered retreat. But the thrill of the challenge, the allure of the idol, and the chance to outwit the High Scythe filled him with reckless determination. He drew a thin, silver dagger—unassuming to the untrained eye, but imbued with the blessing of the Agothian fey, capable of severing the threads of soul magic. With a roguish grin, he whispered, “Time for one last dance.”

Gregan lunged forward, moving like a shadow between the flickering lights. His blade met the staff of the High Scythe with a resounding clash, sending sparks into the air. The chamber erupted into chaos as the other clerics joined the fray. The scent of burning incense mixed with the metallic tang of blood as the thief fought with the grace of a dancer, every strike precise and calculated.

In the heart of the melee, Gregan spun and vaulted onto the altar, seizing the Dark Idol with both hands. Its surface was icy cold, and a wave of dark energy surged through him, making his skin crawl. He felt a brief moment of triumph as he lifted the relic free—until the room fell silent, and a cold wind swept through the chamber.

The Scythes stepped back; their chanting halted. The High Scythe’s mask tilted slightly, and Gregan saw a glint of amusement in her eyes. “You’ve taken what is not yours, thief,” she intoned, her voice echoing with a power beyond mortal comprehension. The ground beneath Gregan began to crack, and tendrils of shadow coiled around his legs, pulling him down into the earth.

Gregan’s smirk faltered, but he tightened his grip on the idol. He had one last trick up his sleeve. With a flick of his wrist, he smashed a vial of blessed oil against the relic, disrupting the soul-binding magic. The shadows recoiled, and a shocked gasp rippled through the chamber as he sprang towards the archway, the idol clutched tightly to his chest.

The High Scythe’s laughter echoed through the temple as Gregan sprinted into the night, her mocking voice trailing behind him like a ghostly whisper. Bells rang out through the darkened streets of Aequus, sounding the alarm. But the thief had already vanished into the maze of alleyways and rooftops that made up the city’s sprawling underbelly.

Whether he had secured a treasure beyond measure or cursed himself with a relic of death, only time would tell. For now, Gregan Tainlel had pulled off the heist of a lifetime, outwitting the Scythes and escaping the clutches of Malkurath’s devoted. It was a feat that would be whispered about in the taverns of the Numari Empire for years to come, a tale of daring and skill that solidified his reputation as the greatest thief the empire had ever known.

GETTING STARTED

The Traris Roleplaying Game (TRG) offers an experience like no other, immersing players in a world of mythical adventure where great heroes—or cunning villains—come together to pursue epic goals within a dynamic campaign setting. As a player, you’ll create a unique character and collaborate with fellow adventurers, embarking on quests and overcoming challenges as a team. For those who choose the role of Gamesmaster, TRG offers the opportunity to craft vast, imaginative worlds where your players can explore the limits of what’s possible.

In an era dominated by computers (and, admittedly, I’m writing this on one), it’s easy to let graphics and sound effects fill the space where our imagination once thrived. Yet, a roleplaying game like TRG rekindles the spark of creativity, inviting us to step beyond the constraints of programmed experiences. In a video game, no matter how advanced, you’ve likely encountered moments where you wondered what lay behind a locked door, wished you could interact with a particular item, or yearned to confront a background character.

These limitations are where TRG truly shines—unlike computer games, a roleplaying game has no boundaries. It empowers you to explore anything you can imagine, without the restrictions of pre-set programming. Whether you’re a seasoned adventurer or new to the world of tabletop roleplaying, TRG opens the door to infinite possibilities. So, let’s dive in and see what it takes to embark on this journey of imagination and creativity.

PLAYER CHARACTER

If you're reading this book, chances are you’re preparing to take on the role of a player in the Traris Roleplaying Game. Your task is to create a unique character and step into their shoes as you navigate the campaign crafted by your Gamesmaster. In the upcoming chapters, you’ll discover everything you need to know to build your character and breathe life into them throughout the game.

A Player Character (often abbreviated as PC) is one of the protagonists of the story. Your character will likely be part of a team (although solo adventures are possible) working together to complete quests, grow in power, and perhaps even confront the gods themselves. It’s an exciting journey filled with opportunities for adventure and heroics.

To play the Traris Roleplaying Game, you’ll need a set of polyhedral dice. While most board games only use six-sided dice, this game requires a wider variety, with the primary roll being made using a twenty-sided die (d20). You may also need other dice, such as four-sided (d4), six-sided (d6), eight-sided (d8), ten-sided (d10), and twelve-sided (d12) dice for various situations and special checks throughout the game.

You can find these specialty dice at your local game store or online. Additionally, you’ll need a character sheet (a copy is included at the back of this book for personal use), as well as a pencil or pen. It’s also helpful to have some scrap paper on hand for notes and maps. To keep track of important details, consider investing in a sturdy notebook—it can be a valuable tool for storing your notes and keeping your adventures organized.

THE BASIC RULES

TRG Prime offers a foundation for your imagination to thrive. It provides rules to define your character’s abilities, guide your storytelling decisions, and resolve conflicts between characters and the obstacles they encounter.

THE CORE RULES

TRG Prime uses a streamlined core system to resolve actions. Whenever your character attempts any action with a chance of failure, follow these steps:

1. Roll a twenty-sided die (abbreviated d20).

2. Add any relevant modifiers (such as abilities, skills, and situational bonuses).

3. Compare the total to a number called the action’s Difficulty (DC), a value set by the GM based on the situation.

If the result equals or exceeds the Difficulty, the action is a success. If the result is lower than the Difficulty, the action fails. This straightforward system is used for almost everything in TRG Prime, with adjustments based on modifiers, the set Difficulty, and the effects of success or failure.

THE GAMESMASTER (GM)

In a TRG Prime game, one player takes on the role of Gamesmaster, abbreviated as GM throughout the rules. The GM is responsible for running the game, acting as a blend of writer, director, and referee. It’s a significant responsibility, but also a highly rewarding one, as the GM gets to craft the setting, bring its characters to life, and create engaging, memorable storylines for the players to explore.

PLAYER CHARACTERS (PC)

The other players in a TRG Prime game create the protagonists of the story—the central figures of an ongoing adventure series, much like the heroes of a novel or a serial narrative. As a player, you’ll craft your character using the guidelines provided in this book, with support and guidance from your GM, allowing you to build the kind of character you want to play. The process involves several key components, which are briefly outlined here and explained in detail in the following chapters.

ABILITY SCORES

In TRG Prime, all player characters (PCs) have core ability scores that define their capabilities. These ability scores are:

Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma.

Higher ability scores provide bonuses (+1 to +5), while lower scores impose penalties (down to -5). These scores impact your d20 rolls for core actions.

During character creation, you’ll determine how strong, agile, tough, intelligent, wise, and charismatic your character is by selecting their ability scores. Detailed steps for generating your character are outlined later in this chapter.

OPEN ENDEDMany of the checks that are made in the game will be open-ended. This involves rolling the dice again if a high or low result is made on the initial check. Open-ended checks are explained in more detail in the next section.OPEN ENDEDMany of the checks that are made in the game will be open-ended. This involves rolling the dice again if a high or low result is made on the initial check. Open-ended checks are explained in more detail in the next section.

RACE & BACKGROUND

In TRG Prime, each player character (PC) begins by choosing a race and a background. Race serves as a crucial foundation, shaping your character’s origins and providing a starting point for the rest of the character creation process. It also sets the tone for your character’s growth and development throughout the game.

Your character’s background, on the other hand, explains their past and roots, adding depth to their story. It also grants key abilities and skills that reflect their upbringing and life experiences before the adventure begins.

CHARACTER CLASS

In TRG Prime, player characters (PCs) choose from one of eight distinct character classes, categorized into three main types: Adept, Expert, and Martial. Each class defines the role your character plays in the story, shaping their abilities, strengths, and the way they interact with the world around them.

SKILLS

In TRG Prime, skills represent a character’s competency in specific tasks or areas of knowledge, such as acrobatics, diplomacy, riding, or stealth. Skills are measured in ranks, representing a character’s level of training in a given skill. Each rank grants a +1 bonus when a PC attempts an action related to that skill. Players select their PC’s skills from a list of available options. For more details, see Chapters 3 & 4.

FEATS

Feats in TRG Prime are special abilities that represent unique talents or advanced training. They allow your PC to perform actions beyond the capabilities of others or grant specific advantages in certain situations. You choose your PC’s feats based on the abilities you want them to have, tailoring their strengths to fit your playstyle. As your character levels up and grows, they acquire additional feats. For more details, see Chapter 5: Feats.

DICE ROLLS

There are a number of different die rolls in TRG, although they all follow the core system of a d20 roll plus modifiers versus a Difficulty.

The three main die rolls are checks, attack rolls, and saving throws.

CHECKS

To make a check in TRG Prime, roll a d20 and add your modifier for the relevant trait (such as an ability or skill). The goal is to roll as high as possible. Rolling a natural 20 (a roll of 20 before adding modifiers) is not an automatic success, and rolling a natural 1 (a roll of 1 before adding modifiers) is not an automatic failure—except in the case of attack rolls, which follow different rules (see Attack Rolls later in this Introduction and Chapter 7 for more details).

Check = d20 + modifier versus Difficulty

GLOSSARY OF TERMS

TRG Prime uses various terms and abbreviations that you’ll become familiar with as you play. Below is a summary of the most frequently used terms.

ABILITY SCORE

Each creature has six ability scores: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma. These scores represent a creature's basic attributes. Higher scores provide bonuses, while lower scores result in penalties.

ACTION

An action is something that the character can do and generally has an Action Point cost assigned to it. Casting spells, attacking an opponent and climbing a wall are all examples of an action.

ACTION POINT (AP)

Each character begins a tactical round with a set amount of Action Points (AP) usually 3. Actions in combat will have a set amount of AP that must be expended to use them. Certain conditions and abilities can change this number.

ADVANTAGE

When you have advantage on a d20 roll, you roll twice and use the higher result. Advantage can also apply to certain d100 checks, allowing you to select the more favourable die as the tens digit.

ATTACK BONUS (AB)

Attack Bonus measures the overall effectiveness of your attacks with a given weapon, spell or ability. In other words, the Attack Bonus is the number you add to your dice roll when your character performs an attack.

Attack Bonus is calculated using the following formula:

Attack Bonus = base attack bonus + ability score + other bonuses + penalties.

ATTACK ROLL

To make an attack, roll a d20 and add your AB along with any relevant modifiers. If the total meets or exceeds your target’s Defensive Bonus (DB), you successfully hit and deal damage. If your attack value is 5 or greater, you have inflicted a critical hit to your target (see below).

ATTACK VALUE (AV)

This value represents the amount that your attack roll has exceeded your targets Defensive Bonus by. If this value is a certain value (usually 5 or more), then you have inflicted a critical hit to your target.

BASE ATTACK BONUS (BAB)

BAB is a numerical value that represents your combat training and skill in melee and ranged combat. It measures your proficiency and effectiveness in landing successful attacks with weapons. This attribute increases in line with your level and is determined by your character class.

BASE DEFENCE BONUS (BDB)

BDB is a numerical value that represents your ability to avoid blows. This attribute increases in line with your level and is determined by your character class.

BASE SPELL BONUS (BSB)

BSB is a numerical value that represents your ability to cast spells. This attribute increases in line with your level and is determined by your character class.

BONUS

Bonuses are numerical values that are added to checks and statistical scores. Most bonuses have a type, and as a rule, bonuses of the same type are not cumulative (do not “stack”)—only the greater bonus granted applies.

CASTER LEVEL

The total caster level of a character which is used to determine the power level of magic (if any) that they can use.

CHECK

A roll made using a d20 or d100 to determine the outcome of an action. Most checks use d20, while certain advanced checks may use a d100.

CRITICAL HIT

When you successfully strike a target, you may inflict a critical hit. The severity of the critical is based upon your Attack Value (AV).

DAMAGE

Damage is inflicted to a targets Hit Points score from a successful attack.

DAMAGE REDUCTION (DR)

This value is provided by your armour and natural armour and determines how resilient you are to damage.

DEATH STATE

Death State is a fixed character attribute that sets how much Dying a creature can endure before it dies: in TRG, most characters have a Death State of 5 (rarely 4 for unusually frail characters or 6 for exceptionally resilient ones), and whenever a character has the Dying (X) condition they die immediately if their Dying value ever becomes greater than their Death State; check this threshold any time Dying changes (from the start-of-turn Dying Check, taking damage while Dying, failed stabilization, or other effects).

DEFENSIVE BONUS (DB)

Defensive Bonus (DB) is a special difficulty which determines how hard it is for your character to be struck with an attack during combat. As with other Difficulty Checks (DC, see below), the attacker must equal or exceed your DB to score a successful hit on you.

Defensive Bonus is calculated using the following formula:

Defensive Bonus = base defence bonus + Dex + armour modifier + other bonuses + penalties.

BASE DEFENCE

Every character has a Base Defence score which is equal to 10 + class Base Defence Bonus (BDB).

DICE & DICE ROLLS

Most dice rolls and checks that you will make will involve a d20. Other dice will be used from time to time (such as a d6 or d12).

Dice (d4, d6, d8, d10, d12, d20, and d%)

When the lowercase letter d is followed by a number, it refers to a die with that many sides. For example, a d6 is a six-sided die, and a d20 is a 20-sided die. Sometimes you roll multiple dice and add them together; in these cases, the number of dice goes in front of the “d” and the type of die goes after it. For example, 4d6 means “roll four six-sided dice and add them together.”

d% rolls

This means rolling two ten-sided dice, possibly of different colour, and counting one of them as the tens and the other as units (of course deciding before rolling which die will be the tens, and which the units).

So, a roll showing up a “5” on the tens die and a “7” on the units die will read as a “57”; a “3” and a “9” as a “39” and “0” and a “4” as a “04” - or simply “4”.

The exception to this is double zeroes, which does not read as a “0” but instead as a “100”.

This way, the two dice combined can produce any result within the 1 and 100 range.

DIFFICULTY CHECK (DC)

Whenever you attempt to perform an action where a success is not guaranteed, you must make some sort of check (usually a skill check). That check is assigned a difficulty by the GM which is referred to as a DC.

DISADVANTAGE

When you have disadvantage on a d20 roll, roll twice and use the lower result. For d100 checks, choose the less favourable die as the tens digit.

EFFECTIVE LEVEL (EL)

This terminology is used for describing the level of a creature. A creature may be more powerful or less powerful than its actual Level and so this value represents its level relative to PC’s.

EXPERIENCE POINTS (XP)

As a character overcomes challenges, defeats monsters, and completes quests, he gains experience points. These points accumulate over time, and when they reach or surpass a specific value, the character gains a level.

FEAT

A feat is an ability which is selected by a creature or character. Feats represent special skills and abilities that help develop an individual creature.

GAME MASTER (GM)

A Game Master is the person who adjudicates the rules and controls all the elements of the story and world that the players explore. A GM's duty is to provide a fair and fun game. The game’s storyteller, referee, and director.

HIT POINTS (HP)

Each character has an amount of HP based upon their size, class, Con and then any modifiers for feats and abilities.

INITIATIVE

Whenever combat begins, all creatures involved in the battle must make an initiative check to determine the order in which creatures act during combat. The higher the result of the check, the earlier a creature gets to act. Initiative is a d100 roll + (Dex x5) + (Wis x5) + any bonus modifiers. The higher the result, the earlier you can act.

LEVEL

The total level of a character.

LEVEL DC

This is a static DC based upon the characters level and a static modifier of 14, often used to resist severe critical effects.

Level DC = level + 14

LINE OF EFFECT (LOE)

A line of effect is a straight, unblocked path that indicates what a spell can affect. A line of effect is cancelled by a solid barrier. It's like line of sight for ranged weapons, except that it's not blocked by fog, darkness, and other factors that limit normal sight. A line of effect starts from any corner of your square and extends to the limit of its range or until it strikes a barrier that would block it. A line-shaped spell affects all creatures in squares through which the line passes.

LINE OF SIGHT (LOS)

A line of sight is the same as a Line of Effect but with the additional restriction that that it is blocked by fog, darkness, and other factors that limit normal sight (such as Concealment).

MELEE ATTACK

An attack in hand-to-hand combat. A basic melee attack is a d20 roll + your attack bonus.

METAGAMING

This is when characters act on information that they don’t have access to, but which their players know from the real world. Metagaming comes into play when players fail to maintain a divide between in-character knowledge and out-of-character knowledge. That could include anything from uncannily accurate in-character predictions from a player who’s already read the adventure, players recognizing monsters when their characters wouldn’t, low-Intelligence characters accessing well-educated players’ knowledge and feats, etc.

NON-PLAYER CHARACTER (NPC)

This is a character played by the Gamemaster (not one of the other players), such as a city guard or innkeeper, or even a monster such as a goblin.

OPEN ENDED ROLLS

When rolling a d20, an open-ended roll means there is no absolute minimum or maximum. First, roll a d20; if the result is 20, roll again and add the new result to the first roll. If the second roll is also 20, roll again and continue adding until a roll other than 20 is made. The total sum of these rolls is the result of the open-ended roll.

Marcus is deep in conversation with a local street thug and makes a Detect Deception (Sense Motive) check to determine if the thug is lying to him. Marcus has a bonus of +17 in the Sense Motive skill and rolls a d20 getting a result of 20. Marcus rolls the dice again and this time gets another 20, thus allowing him to roll again. His third dice roll is a 5 so he rolls no further dice. His total for his check is 17 + 20 + 20 + 5 = 62.

If the first d20 roll is a 1, the dice are rolled again and the result subtracted from the first roll. If the second roll is 20, then a third roll is made and subtracted, and so on until a non 20 roll is made. The total of these rolls is the result of the low open-ended roll. A roll of 1 on anything other than the first roll does not cause one to roll again.

After Marcus achieved a remarkable Heroic success on his Detect Deception check, he uncovers the street thug's hidden secret: the king's daughter is being kept in his basement. Marcus, seizing the opportunity, decides to employ his Bluff (Deception) skill to trick the thug into believing that he is a devoted servant of the girl, urgently needing to speak with her. With an impressive +11 bonus in Deception, Marcus rolls a 1 on his d20 check, triggering a low open-ended roll. His subsequent roll yields a 20, necessitating another roll. Finally, he rolls a 3, which marks the end of the roll sequence. As a result, Marcus achieves a total check of 11 + 1 - 20 - 3 = -11. It appears Marcus may encounter a significant challenge ahead.

Sometimes an open-ended roll may be bottom-ended or top-ended. If this is the case, the roll will only continue in one direction.

When rolling a d%, the same percentage chance remains so a roll of 96-100 indicates that the dice are rolled again and the result added to the first roll and a roll of 01-05 the next die subtracted.

CHAOS RESULTWhen using open-ended checks with a d20, a GM may introduce an element of chaos if a 1 is rolled immediately after an open-ended 20 or 1. This result triggers an unpredictable outcome, determined by the context of the check.For d100 rolls, the same rule applies if a 66 is rolled on the initial check, introducing a chaotic or unexpected effect based on the situation.CHAOS RESULTWhen using open-ended checks with a d20, a GM may introduce an element of chaos if a 1 is rolled immediately after an open-ended 20 or 1. This result triggers an unpredictable outcome, determined by the context of the check.For d100 rolls, the same rule applies if a 66 is rolled on the initial check, introducing a chaotic or unexpected effect based on the situation.

PLAYER CHARACTER (PC)

This is a character directly controlled by one of the players—typically a hero of the story you're playing.

POWER POINTS (PP)

Power points are used when you cast spells. If you have no PP you cannot cast a spell.

RANGED ATTACK

An attack with a projectile weapon, such as a bow and arrow. A basic ranged attack is a d20 roll + your ranged attack bonus.

ROUND

Combat is measured in rounds. During an individual round, all creatures have one turn which is taken in initiative order.

ROUNDING

Occasionally the rules ask you to round a result or value. Unless otherwise stated, always round down. For example, if you are asked to take half of 7, the result would be 3.

SAVING THROW

When a creature is the subject of a dangerous spell or effect, it often receives a saving throw to mitigate the damage or result. Saving throws are passive, meaning that a character does not need to take an action to make a saving throw—they are made automatically. There are three types of saving throw: Fortitude (used to resist poisons, diseases, and other bodily ailments), Reflex (used to avoid area attacks) and Will (used to resist mental attacks and spells).

BASIC SAVING THROW

Sometimes you will be asked to make a basic saving throw which follows the below format:

Critical The target is unaffected.

Success The target takes half damage.

Partial The target takes full damage.

Failure As partial but the target also takes additional base damage and a critical based upon how much they fail by.

LEVEL BASED SAVING THROW

If you are asked to make a level-based saving throw, this is usually a DC based upon the level of the effect (or creature) that you are resisting. If there is no attacking creature or effect, the saving throw is made against your Level DC.

SKILL

A representation of a character’s training in specific tasks or knowledge. Skills always have a tier of proficiency.

SKILL CHECK

Your ability to do something, from lying to climbing a wall or healing wounds. A skill check is a d20 roll + your skill modifier from the related skill (if any).

SPEED

Represents how many feet a creature can move using a single Action Point at walking pace. This is usually a land speed, but maybe another type of movement such as swim or fly.

SPELLCRAFT

The ability to cast spells is represented by a special attribute called Spellcraft. To determine your Spellcraft attribute, add your Base Spell Bonus (BSB) to your tradition ability score. This may be modified further by feats and abilities.

TURN

In a round, a creature receives one turn, during which it can perform a wide variety of actions. Over the course of a creatures turn it can usually carry out 3 Action Points worth of actions.

SPECIAL TEXT TYPES

Throughout the rulebook you will come across a number of pieces of text which are colour coded. Each one has a different purpose as explained below:

BE AWARE

Text of this type generally gives the player a warning and advises of a rule or option which must be abided by.

EXAMPLE

Text of this type gives an example of a specific rule in use.

EMPHASIS

Text of this type draws attention to a specific rule and emphasises a point of interest.

OPTIONAL

Text of this type describes an optional rule or ruleset which must be authorised by your GM before use.

CHARACTER CREATION

Beyond the statistics and numbers on your character sheet lies the core of who your character truly is. It’s time to dive into your character’s identity. First, consider their name, gender, and origin. What name do they go by, and from where do they hail? Your GM can provide examples of common names and cultural backgrounds to help you choose, while in a well-defined setting, your place of birth may also shape your character’s appearance and personality. In a more open-ended fantasy world, feel free to create a name that resonates with you, inspired perhaps by a favourite novel or film. Adding details about your character’s backstory will enrich the narrative and seamlessly fit into a variety of adventures.

Next, think about your character’s appearance. How do they look? A vivid and detailed description of their physical features will serve as an anchor in the story, helping both the GM and fellow players visualize your character within the unfolding world. Consider their hair colour, build, distinguishing marks, or style of dress—anything that makes them stand out.

Now, delve into your character’s personality and the experiences that shaped it. What is their outlook on life? What are their greatest hopes and deepest fears? What is their relationship with their family, and where do they reside now? Do they have siblings or children? This part of your character’s description can be as complex as you like, representing the intricate layers of who they are. However, you don’t need to define everything immediately—let some aspects evolve naturally as the game progresses, giving you the chance to discover new depths to your character.

As you develop your character concept, think about what makes them stand out in a world filled with fantastical beings and legendary heroes. What qualities set them apart? What will Bards and storytellers remember first about your character? Keep in mind, though, that striving to be overly unique can sometimes make it hard for others to connect with your character. A couple of distinct traits are enough. These might include physical features (such as striking eye colour, a distinctive tattoo, or a unique piece of clothing), personality quirks (a particular mannerism, an intriguing character flaw, or an unusual phobia), or habits (a love of clever wordplay, a taste for exotic foods, or bouts of unexpected luck). Before you decide on these distinguishing features, check with your GM to ensure they fit well with the game’s setting and tone.

Once you have a clear concept in mind, you’re ready to begin the character creation process, which consists of seven fundamental steps.

STEP 1: ABILITY SCORES

Every character (PC or NPC) possesses inherent abilities that shape their actions and capabilities. These ability scores have a profound impact on nearly every aspect of your character's endeavours. Greater strength allows for impressive feats of might, heightened dexterity grants enhanced agility and balance, increased constitution grants resilience to endure hardships, and so on.

There are six primary abilities that define a character: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma. The trio of Strength, Dexterity, and Constitution represents physical prowess, while Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma encompass mental faculties. Having an above-average score in these abilities bestows bonuses on certain dice rolls, while below-average scores impose penalties on specific rolls. These ability scores serve as the foundation upon which your character's capabilities are built, influencing their interactions and outcomes within the game world.

CHOOSING ABILITY SCORES

Each ability score is assigned a numerical value that represents a corresponding bonus or penalty, ranging from -5 (signifying abysmal or disabled) to +5 or higher (indicating legendary or superhuman abilities), with an average score of 0. When ability scores are referenced in the rule book, the score is specified alongside the name of the ability, such as Strength 2 or Dexterity -1.

At character creation, you are given 6 points to distribute among your ability scores, all of which begin at 0 with no inherent bonus or penalty. This allows for various allocation options, such as having 1 in each of the six abilities, having 3 in one ability while leaving two abilities at 0 and distributing the remaining 5 across the other three abilities, or any combination that adds up to 6. The only restriction is that no ability score can exceed 4 points. (ability scores can increase beyond 4 through level advancement and specific factors.)

If you opt for a negative value in an ability score, you gain bonus points that can be allocated to bolster your other ability scores. This provides flexibility in customizing your character's strengths and weaknesses within the allocated point total.

Lewi assigns Gilbert a Strength –2, this gives him 2 more points to assign to other ability scores.

You cannot have abilities lower than –4, and abilities lower than –2 aren’t recommended unless you are seriously deficient in that ability. Even with bonus points, you cannot put more than 4 points in a single ability score.

Your ability score is added to or subtracted from die rolls when you do something related to that ability. Your Strength score affects the amount of melee damage you do, your Intelligence score affects your Recall Knowledge checks, and so forth. Sometimes your score is used to calculate another value, such as when you use your Dexterity score to help determine how good you are at avoiding harm using your reflexes (your Reflex saving throw).

Be aware that although abilities cannot be started above 4 through the expenditure of ability points, racial modifiers do allow an ability to exceed 4.

You can also use your level-based ability score increases to bring a base ability above 4 to a maximum of 6 (before other modifiers such as racial and magic).

THE ABILITY SCORES

Given here are descriptions of the six ability scores and how they affect your character.

STRENGTH (STR)

Strength measures a character's physical power, muscle, and raw physical force. It influences carrying capacity, melee attack rolls, and damage dealt with melee weapons. This ability score is important for those who engage in hand-to-hand (or “melee”) combat. Strength also sets the maximum amount of weight your character can carry. A character with a Strength score of -5 is too weak to move in any way and is unconscious.

DEXTERITY (DEX)

Dexterity represents a character's agility, reflexes, and hand-eye coordination. It affects ranged attack rolls, DB, initiative, and certain skills associated with agility and finesse. This ability is vital for characters seeking to excel with ranged weapons, such as the bow or sling. A character with a Dexterity score of -5 is incapable of moving and is effectively immobile (but not unconscious).

CONSTITUTION (CON)

Constitution reflects a character's overall health, endurance, and resilience. It influences HP, Fortitude saving throws, and determines the character's ability to withstand physical hardships and endure conditions. As Constitution increases a character's HP, it is an important ability score for all classes. A character with a Constitution score of -5 is dead.

INTELLIGENCE (INT)

Intelligence represents a character's intellect, knowledge, and cognitive abilities. It affects the character's skill ranks, the number of languages they can learn, and their ability to solve puzzles, recall information, and reason logically. This ability is important for wizards because it affects their spellcasting ability in many ways. Creatures of animal-level instinct have Intelligence scores of -4 or -3. Any creature capable of understanding speech has a score of at least -2. A character with an Intelligence score of -5 is comatose (unless it is mindless).

WISDOM (WIS)

Wisdom reflects a character's perception, intuition, and common sense. It influences Will saving throws, certain skills related to awareness, and spellcasting ability for classes that rely on wisdom. If you want your character to have acute senses, put a high score in Wisdom. A character with a Wisdom score of -5 is incapable of rational thought and is unconscious.

CHARISMA (CHA)

Charisma measures a character's force of personality, charm, and ability to influence others. It affects social interactions, diplomacy, bluffing, and certain spellcasting abilities for classes that rely on charisma. A character with a Charisma score of -5 is not able to exert himself in any way and is unconscious.

STEP 2: RACE

In TRG, race holds significant importance, serving as a foundation for character creation and shaping the character's journey. It intertwines biology and culture, blending them into distinct racial traits. However, the malleability of both biology and culture, particularly under the influence of powerful magic, allows for diverse manifestations of racial traits. As a result, even among the same race, two individuals can exhibit remarkable differences while still reflecting aspects of their shared heritage and culture. A race's unique traits, rich history, interrelationships with other races, and the culture that emanates from these factors all contribute to the framework of your character, shaping their identity and experiences.

The races available are detailed briefly below and in more detail in Chapter 2: Races & Backgrounds.

Ascendan: There are several ancient races in the world, but none are more mysterious than this unusual and secretive race of humanoids. Sometimes referred to as the first race, or Alphar, the Ascendan are widely believed to be the oldest of the humanoid races.

Dwarf: Dwarves possess unparalleled craftsmanship skills, creating exquisite works of artistry that showcase their remarkable talent. Their deep appreciation for precious stones and metals further enhances their craft. Typically, dwarves choose to reside in proximity to regions abundant with these resources, establishing grand mountain complexes and vast subterranean settlements as their homes.

Elf: Elves have a strong connection with the natural world around them; they strive to always live in harmony with it. Elves see magic as simply another aspect of nature and have a natural flare when it comes to using it. Due to their immortal nature, Elves often wander away from a project that they are working on, only to return to it decades or even centuries later. This aloof attitude is often misunderstood by other races, and as a lack of self-discipline.

Gnome: Gnomes spend their days solving puzzles and mysteries. Knowledge is sought above all else and many members of the race have simply packed up and left their homeland in the pursuit of knowledge. Magic is the pinnacle of all knowledge, so it is not uncommon to find Gnomish spell casters of all sorts. Gnomes can also be quite secretive and generally hide their settlements away from the prying eyes of other races.

Halfling: Halflings are incurable opportunists. They rarely think ahead for more than a few minutes, and their plans more often than not go wrong. They are not the strongest of individuals and have long discovered methods to get around situations without resorting to the use of brute force.

Human: The most widespread of all civilized races are humans, Humans strive to expand, constantly pushing the limits of what they are capable of. Unfortunately, this drive to succeed throws them into sometime hostile situations with other races and other humans.

Kornargon: Once a race a race of humanoids native to the prime plane, this race were exiled for reasons unknown into the Plane of Shadow. They are creatures born into the darkness, but not necessarily creatures of evil. Honour and family are the two most important aspects of Kornargon life, and these are upheld above all other things.

Orc: Aggressive, callous, and domineering. Bullies by nature, they respect strength and power as the highest virtues. On an almost instinctive level, orcs believe they are entitled to anything they want unless someone stronger can stop them from seizing it. Powerfully built, orcs typically stand just a few inches taller than most humans but have much greater muscle mass, their broad shoulders and thick, brawny hips often giving them a slightly lurching gait. They typically have dulled green skin, coarse dark hair, beady red eyes, and protruding, tusk-like teeth. Orcs consider scars a mark of distinction and frequently use them as a form of body art.

STEP 3: BACKGROUND

Your background helps mould your character further and provides an insight into your early experiences. Although every character has a class, there are a myriad of ways that you can progress throughout your career. A background expands your choices and adds unique abilities which further individualise your character.

When you create your character at 1st level you select one background of your choice. Once your background selection is made, it cannot be amended at higher levels so choose wisely. Your selected background will grant you a bonus feat, a +1-class bonus to three specific skills and a specialist skill.

Some backgrounds may also offer additional abilities which will be detailed in their descriptions.

STEP 4: CHARACTER CLASS

A character's class represents their skillset and core abilities. Your class will determine what skill groups you specialise in, what class feats you have access to and any other abilities. As you gain experience points (XP) for defeating monsters, roleplaying and overcoming various obstacles you will progress in level, gaining new powers and abilities.

LEVEL

Your level measures your overall power on a scale of 1 to 20 (and possibly beyond) and helps the GM determine appropriate challenges for you and your party. Most campaigns begin at level 1 with each Player Character possessing 10,000 Experience Points (XP).

It is assumed that starting characters would have already gained a certain level of expertise just by achieving level 1 in their class.

Some games may start at a higher level, in which case each character should start with the same amount of XP (determined by the GM).

As you complete adventures your total XP rises. Each time your total XP reaches the amount needed for the next level it goes up by 1 and you gain all of the benefits shown on the Level Table (see below). At this time, you also gain any new benefits associated with your character class for progressing a level.

Levelling requires a brief period to reflect and train. You may generally only do so between adventures and during Downtime.

The Level Table details several key abilities for your character.

Total XP: The amount of experience points required to achieve the indicated level.

Class Bonus: This bonus is added to any class skills that you have.

Ability Increase: At 3rd level and then every three levels thereafter, you may increase any one of your ability scores by +1.

Be aware that you may not increase the base value of an ability score above 6 with ability score increases.

Feats: This is the number of feats you may choose from either general or specialist feats for your class.

Classes are explained in more detail in Chapter 3: Classes.

STEP 5: SKILL RANKS

Skill ranks are bought and improved with points granted by classes. You may buy ranks in any skill, but certain skills are class skills and gain the class bonus.

Each rank costs 1 skill point. The maximum number of ranks that you may have in any one skill is equal to your level.

Be Aware that if you cannot spend all your skill points when you gain a level, excess points are wasted and cannot be carried over.

STEP 6: FEATS

You must now make a note of any feats that you have gained from your race, background and class.

All racial bonus and background feats are added to your character automatically. You must also select one unique racial feat.

Your character class will then assign several additional feats which are added automatically. Any further feats which you may select must be picked from those available to you from your racial feats, general feats or class feats.

You will gain at least one additional feat each time you gain a level of experience. These again must be selected from those available to you.

STEP 7: FINAL TOUCHES

There are a few other tasks which you must complete before your character is ready to go.

SAVING THROWS

Generally, when you are subject to an unusual or magical attack, you get a saving throw to avoid or reduce the effect. Like an attack roll, a saving throw is a d20 roll plus a bonus based on your training, and an associated ability score.

Your saving throw modifier is:

Base save bonus + ability modifier + other modifiers

SAVING THROW TYPES

The three different kinds of saving throws are Fortitude, Reflex and Will:

Fortitude

These saves measure your ability to stand up to physical punishment or attacks against your vitality and health. Apply your Constitution modifier to your Fortitude saving throws.

Reflex

These saves test your ability to dodge area attacks and unexpected situations. Apply your Dexterity modifier to your Reflex saving throws.

Will

These saves reflect your resistance to mental influence as well as many magical effects. Apply your Wisdom modifier to your Will saving throws.

STARTING GEAR

Your character begins play with equipment relative to his background. It would be assumed that most characters would begin play with relevant gear and items.

If you would prefer to purchase gear, you start with ana mount of lions (gold pieces) as determined in chapter 6.

OTHER DETAILS

You need to determine your starting initiative, hit points, defence, attack bonus, power points, conviction and personal details.

Initiative

Your initiative score is a major factor in determining how quickly you act in combat.

Your initiative modifier is:

Dexterity x5 + Wisdom x5 + Other Modifiers

Hit Points

Hit Points (HP) allow you to resist physical punishment and direct damage.

Your hit points are determined as follows:

Size Modifier + Con (per level) + Class Mod (per level) + Other Modifiers.

Defence

Your Defence (DB) represents how hard it is for opponents to hit you, the Difficulty for an opponent’s attack roll.

Your defence is determined as follows:

10 + BDB + Dex Bonus + Other Modifiers

Attack Bonus

Your attack bonus (AB) is your ability to hit targets. You must equal or exceed your targets defence with an attack check.

Your attack bonus is determined as follows:

BAB + Str Bonus (or Dex Bonus) + Other Modifiers

Power Points

If you are a spellcaster you will gain an amount of power points (PP) each level which you may use to cast spells.

Your power points are determined as follows:

Race Bonus + Class Bonus + Other Modifiers

Conviction

You begin play with a pool of 1 conviction point. Some characters may gain a bonus to this value.

Languages

You gain languages based upon your race and intelligence score.

Personal Details

Personal details provide specific characteristics that help define your physicality and identity.

Age determines the stage of life you are in, from youthful exuberance to seasoned wisdom.

Weight and height establishes your physical stature, whether you possess a slender or robust build, and your overall presence in the world.

Gender shapes your identity and role in society, influencing how you are perceived and the experiences you navigate.

Together, these personal details add depth and nuance to your character, allowing them to be uniquely envisioned and brought to life within TRG.
