CHAPTER 7 – COMBAT

The cavern was still, the air no longer seething with heat and malice. Only the slow drip of moisture from ancient stone broke the silence. Ember was dead — and yet the mountain did not rest. Marcus, ever cautious, studied the hoard, now eerily quiet. He stepped lightly over bones and melted gold, his fingers brushing ancient relics, scrolls, and talismans. “No dragon,” he muttered, “leaves a pile like this unwarded.”

He was right. The moment Hector laid a hand upon a ruby-studded circlet, the entire chamber shuddered. Runes flared crimson along the walls — the last breath of a dragon’s dying curse. Ember, ancient as time itself, had bound her soul to her lair, vowing vengeance should she fall.

A great crack echoed as stone split along the far wall, revealing a hidden passage descending into fire-lit depths.

“I knew it wasn’t over,” Keldax growled, raising his twin swords.

“Something stirs,” Hector murmured, arcane light flickering in his eyes. “Not Ember… something worse.”

They followed the heat, the flickering shadows leading them downward into a shrine wreathed in obsidian and bone. At the centre: a dragon egg, larger than any they had seen, pulsing with life. It floated above a ritual altar, sustained by Ember’s still-flickering soul. A voice echoed through the chamber — not Ember’s roar, but a whisper like fire devouring parchment.

“You have slain the mother. The daughter shall be born in wrath.”

Hector stepped forward, staff glowing. “We must end this now. While we can.”

But Keldax hesitated. “It is not yet a threat. Could… could it be raised to good?”

Marcus raised a brow. “You want to raise a dragon?”

“No,” the orc said, lowering his blades. “I want to redeem one.”

The three stood in uneasy silence. The egg pulsed again, darker now — sensing conflict, sensing choice.

And thus, a new quest began — not of conquest, but of consequence. Would the child of Ember be destruction reborn… or a legend remade?

The adventurers sheathed their weapons. This fight was over. But their story was far from done.

A fantasy roleplaying setting is a dangerous place full of dragons, orcs and other dangers. There will come a time when diplomacy ends and swords are drawn. When such a situation occurs, a series of rules are needed to determine how such events unfold. When not in combat many actions or spells will be used and rolled for with little or minimum duress. As soon as battle breaks out the importance of selecting the correct actions becomes imperative. The first thing that you will hear when combat occurs will often be the GM saying those age-old words, “let’s roll for initiative”.

Combat is a serious thing in any roleplaying game. While characters are assumed to be heroic, even the most skilful fighter must approach combat cautiously because of the high chance of being wounded or killed with a single blow even by less skilled opponents.

ENCOUNTERS

Once a combat begins the tracking of time becomes crucial. Your party will spend the majority of its time investigating surrounding areas, exploring and in other non-combative pursuits. When a combat ensues however, the chaos erupts.

To keep track of what is occurring in a combat, an encounter is broken down into rounds, turns, and actions.

THE STRUCTURE

To resolve encounters a set of rules are needed to govern the process. As soon as an encounter begins, the GM will ask for initiative checks and the game will move into rounds. During each round, the player characters and non-player characters each gain a turn of actions which they may be used in order of sequence based upon their initiative checks. Rounds are played out until the encounter is resolved (usually the defeat of one side or another).

Combat is not the only time that an encounter will be used. Sometimes it is needed for other situations.

ROUNDS

A round is a period of time approximately 6 seconds, in which each character involved in the combat gets to take a turn. Despite the fact that the characters will act in order, it is assumed that they act almost simultaneously.

TURNS

Each character that is currently involved in the combat gets to take 1 turn. A characters turn involves a series of actions which are determined by the amount of action points (usually 3) that the character has to use. All of the turns during the round are carried out in order which is determined by an initiative roll.

ACTIONS

When it’s your turn to act you gain 3 Action Points (AP). You can use single actions (1 AP), short activities (2 AP & 3AP), reactions and free actions (which cost 0 AP). When you’re finished, your turn ends and the character next in the initiative order begins their turn.

STEP 1: ROLL INITIATIVE

To determine the order in which each participant in the combat acts, you make an initiative roll. Each character (including npc) involved in the combat makes a d100 roll and adds their initiative bonus. The character with the highest initiative checks acts first, with each other character acting in descending order. In the result of a tie the character with the highest Wisdom bonus acts first. If the result is still tied then highest Dexterity and then flip a coin.

INITIATIVE

To calculate your Initiative, multiply your Dexterity ability score by 5 and your Wisdom ability score by 5, then add the results together. Additional bonuses from feats or other abilities may also apply.

STEP 2: SURPRISE

If you are unaware of your opponents at the start of a combat you are surprised. The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Stealth checks of anyone hiding with the Perception DCs of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn’t notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

Any character who does not begin the encounter surprised may act in the surprise round (see below).

A surprised character gains the flat-footed condition until the beginning of their turn.

STEP 3: SURPRISE ROUND

Before combat begins properly, any characters who may act in the surprise round may use up to 2 AP worth of actions in Initiative order. Even if you can act in the surprise round, you are still classed as Flat-Footed until you act.

STEP 4: PLAY A ROUND

At the beginning of a round, the character with the highest initiative check acts first. All combatants are considered to be Flat-Footed until they have acted for the first time. The round continues until each character involved in the encounter has taken their turn in initiative order. What a character can do on their turn is detailed below. It is also possible to use reactions and free actions outside their turn.

STEP 4: BEGIN NEXT ROUND

As soon as everyone involved in the encounter has taken their turn, the round ends and a new one begins. All characters stay on the same initiative count and this is not re-rolled. Continue to repeat the round cycle until the encounter comes to an end.

STEP 5: COMBAT ENDS

The encounter comes to an end when one hostile side has been defeated, fled or some form of truce is reached.

THE TURN

You can use actions when it is your turn to act. Sometimes it’s important to note when during your turn something happens, so a turn is divided into three phases.

Be Aware at the beginning of a combat all participants are flat-footed and cannot use any actions until they enter their first Assessment Phase.

PHASE 1: ASSESSMENT PHASE

Many things happen automatically in the assessment phase. This phase of your turn is used for tracking the passage of time for effects that last multiple rounds. In your assessment phase, take these steps in any order you choose:

• If you have created an effect with a duration specified in rounds, the number of remaining rounds is reduced by 1 at this point. If the duration reaches 0, the effect comes to an end.

• You can use a single reaction or free action which has a trigger of “Your turn begins” or something similar.

• If you're dying, make a dying check.

• Do anything else that is specified to happen at the start of your turn, such as regaining Hit Points from fast healing or regeneration.

The last step of phase 1 is always the same.

• Regain your 3 AP and your reaction. If you haven't spent your reaction from your last turn, you lose it. If a condition prevents you from being able to act, you don't regain any actions or your reaction.

PHASE 2: ACTION PHASE

You may use your APs to carry out any actions that are available to you. All 2-AP or 3-AP activities must be completed on your turn.

Once you have spent all 3 of your APs, your turn ends (as described in Step 3) and the next creature’s turn begins.

CARRYING ACTIONS

Your GM may allow you to carry actions from one turn to another. This means that you can begin an action and expend a partial amount of AP at the end of your turn to begin an action, finishing it the next.

The exact details of how this works and what actions you may apply this too will be left to your GM.

PHASE 3: END PHASE

Take the following steps in any order you choose. Play then proceeds to the next creature in the initiative order.

• End any effects that last until the end of your turn.

• If you have a recurring damage condition or any ongoing afflictions you take damage from them and then may make checks to remove them.

• Take any further actions or resolve any other specifics that state they occur at the end of your turn.

ACTIONS

During an encounter, the amount of time it takes to carry out actions becomes very important. Action Points (AP) are used to track the amount of actions that you can carry out during your turn and throughout the entire round.

The actions are briefly summarised below.

Three Actions: Actions which cost 3 AP

Two Actions: Actions which cost 2 AP

One Action: Actions which cost 1 AP

Free Actions: Actions which cost 0 AP technically there is no limit to the amount of free actions you can use in a round, but the GM may prevent you from using too many.

Reactions: You have one reaction a round which resets at the beginning of each of your turns in the Assessment Phase. Some feats and abilities will allow you to take more than one reaction.

Most actions that you use during an encounter will be attack and move actions (although a number of other actions do exist). Attack actions come with some unique rules and are handled in a different way to normal skill checks

ATTACKS & DAMAGE

Attacking your enemies and being attacked by them is a large part of any roleplaying game. In each combat you will get a chance to attack your foes, albeit with weapon or spell.

ATTACK BONUS

Attack Bonus (or AB, for short) measures the overall effectiveness of your attacks with a given weapon, spell or ability. In other words, the AB is the number you add to your dice roll when your character performs an attack.

Attack Bonus is calculated using the following formula:

Attack Bonus = BAB (or BSB) + other bonuses + penalties.

DEFENSIVE BONUS

Defensive Bonus (or DB, for short) is a special difficulty which determines how hard it is for your character to be struck with an attack during combat. As with other DC’s, the attacker must equal or exceed your DB to score a successful hit on you.

Defensive Bonus is calculated using the following formula:

Defensive Bonus = 10 + BDB + Dex Bonus + Other Modifiers

ATTACK ROLL

To make an attack, you make a d20 roll and add your current Attack Bonus (or AB) and any other applicable modifiers.

If the final result of the Attack Roll equals or exceeds your targets DB, you have hit and inflict some kind of damage. The amount that you have exceeded your targets DB by with an attack is called your Attack Value (AV). If your attack value is 5 or greater, you have inflicted (in most cases) a critical hit to your target (see below).

NON-PROFICIENCY

If you do not have proficiency with a weapon or attack, you suffer a -4 penalty to all attacks made with it and check for Fumble on an UM 1 or 2 (see below).

FUMBLE

Each time that you make an attack check, you have a chance to fumble it. If your attack roll is an UM 1 (and in some cases a 2), you have a chance of fumbling the attack. Attack fumbles are explored in greater detail later in this chapter.

UNMODIFIED 1 or 20

If you roll a 1 an unmodified 1 on an attack check, the attack always misses (regardless of the AV). Furthermore, an unmodified 20 on an attack check always hits (regardless of the AV).

MULTIPLE ATTACK PENALTY

If you make more than one attack during your turn, your attacks become less accurate. To represent this, you gain a multiple attack penalty for every attack after the first. The second attack action you take during your turn is subject to a -5 penalty and any subsequent attacks -10. Any action which has the attack trait counts towards the multiple attack penalty including disarm, shove, spells etc.

If a weapon or attack possesses the agile trait, your multiple attack penalty is lowered to -4 and -8 respectively.

The multiple attack penalty applies only during your turn, so you don’t have to keep track of it between turns in the event of a reaction.

ATTACK RESULT

Once the attack roll has been made and the Attack Value (AV) determined, we must ascertain the outcome. There are a number of factors which have to be taken into account at this stage.

ATTACK DAMAGE

If your attack is successful, it will inflict some measure of damage to the target. Damage is determined by the weapon or unarmed attack used or the spell cast. Like checks, damage, especially melee weapon damage, is often adjusted by a number of modifiers, penalties, and bonuses. When determining damage, you take the following steps, explained in detail below.

• Apply the Damage of the attack and apply any modifiers, bonuses, and penalties that apply.

• Determine the damage type.

• Determine if the attack is a critical injury, and if so, apply any critical results, including additional damage (see criticals later in the chapter).

• Apply DR against the damage.

• Apply the target’s immunities, weaknesses, and resistances to the damage.

• If any damage remains, reduce the target’s Hit Points by that amount and apply any critical injury results.

BONUS DAMAGE

The basic die of damage which an attack inflicts is called the attacks base damage. As you become more experienced, you also inflict additional bonus damage with each natural attack or weapon attack. The amount of bonus damage that you inflict is based upon your BAB.

COMBAT DAMAGE TABLE

BAB

Bonus Damage

0-5

-

6-11

+1 base

12-17

+2 base

18-23

+3 base

24+

+4 base

Be aware that Spell have their own base damage rules which are covered in Chapter 9: Magic.

DAMAGE MODIFIERS

A melee or thrown attack gains a damage modifier equal to your Strength ability score. Missile attacks do not usually gain a damage modifier (unless stated otherwise in their description). Spells have their own damage modifiers which are unique to each spell.

CRITICAL HIT

If the Attack Value (AV) of your attack is 5 or greater, then you have inflicted a critical hit to your target. This may trigger certain effects and additional damage. Critical hits and how they work are explored later in this section.

GLANCING BLOW

For greater realism you may want to introduce this rule to make attacks inflict less damage if the Attack Value (AV) is quite low.

If the Attack Value (AV) of your attack is between 0 and 1 you have inflicted a glancing blow to your target. The damage inflicted by a glancing blow is rolled normally and the result halved (round up).

HIT POINTS

Hit Points (HPs) are an abstract measure of the amount of punishment you can take before passing out.

Your HP total is calculated using the following formula:

Hit Points (HP) = Class Mod + Size Mod + Racial Mod + Con Mod + Other

Your character’s Current HPs value is equal to your Total HPs, minus any damage received. Lost HPs can be recovered with rest and healing, but your Current HPs value can never be higher than your Total HPs, save for particular exceptions.

As a player character, when you are reduced to 0 Hit Points, you gain the Dying Condition and may potentially suffer further damage or die.

DAMAGE REDUCTION

Damage Reduction or DR is special type of resistance provided by armour and natural armour. When you take damage from an attack, reduce it by any applicable DR before applying resistances and weaknesses.

CRITICALS

If DR reduces the damage from a critical hit to zero or less, the target takes a subdual critical instead of the normal type.

RESISTANCE

When you have Resistance to a specific type of damage, you take only half the damage from that type. This reduction is applied after all other modifiers, such as bonuses and DR, are calculated.

If you have more than one type of resistance that would apply to the same instance of damage, you may only halve the damage once.

Dondo has Fire Resistance and DR 4. He takes 12 fire damage from an incoming fire attack. He first applies half of his DR to the damage reducing it to 10 and then halves the damage due to his Fire Resistance. Dondo therefore takes 5 fire damage from the attack.

IMMUNITY

If you encounter a creature with an immunity to a specific damage type, they ignore all damage and critical hits caused by it.

WEAKNESS

If you have weakness to a certain type of damage you are more susceptible to attacks that inflict damage of that type. All attacks that inflict damage that you have weakness against are increased by 50%.

PRIMARY & SECONDARY DAMAGE

Sometimes an attack will inflict more than one damage type. The damage with the highest output is always referred to as the primary damage and any other damage secondary.

If you inflict a critical hit when striking with multiple damage types you only inflict one critical hit of the primary damage type, unless a specific ability states otherwise.

DR & MULTIPLE DAMAGE TYPESWhen an attack inflicts multiple damage types, you apply your DR to each type separately. Vesuvian has DR 4 and is hit by an attack with a flaming sword. The attacker rolls a d8+4 for his damage (5 rolled) inflicting 9 slashing damage. The sword also inflicts an additional 1d4 fire damage (3 rolled). Vesuvian therefore takes 5 slashing damage and 1 fire damage (DR halved for a fire attack).DR & MULTIPLE DAMAGE TYPESWhen an attack inflicts multiple damage types, you apply your DR to each type separately. Vesuvian has DR 4 and is hit by an attack with a flaming sword. The attacker rolls a d8+4 for his damage (5 rolled) inflicting 9 slashing damage. The sword also inflicts an additional 1d4 fire damage (3 rolled). Vesuvian therefore takes 5 slashing damage and 1 fire damage (DR halved for a fire attack).

DAMAGE TYPES

There are a number of different damage types in the game, and your attack will determine the damage type(s) that you inflict. Determining the damage type is important when dealing with various resistances, immunities and weaknesses and also critical injuries.

PHYSICAL DAMAGE

This type of damage is usually inflicted by weapons, unarmed strikes, physical hazards and various spells. Physical damage types are bludgeoning, piercing, slashing and subdual.

Bludgeoning damage comes from attacks that deal concussion damage such, as a strike from a hammer or the impact of falling a great distance. Piercing damage is dealt from puncturing weapons and attacks such as bites and spears. Slashing damage is inflicted by weapons and attacks with edges such as axes and swords. Subdual damage comes from unarmed attacks and attacks delivered to purposefully disable an opponent rather than kill them. When inflicting subdual damage, any target you reduce to 0 hit points gains the unconscious condition and does not gain the dying condition.

ENERGY DAMAGE

Spells and magical effects are the main cause of energy damage. Such damage can also be caused by natural effects such as snowstorms or volcanos.

The main types of energy damage are acid, cold, electricity, fire, and sonic.

Acid damage burns in a caustic manner and is often inflicted by gases, liquids, and flesh dissolving solids.

Cold damage freezes what it comes into contact and is usually inflicted by area spells and effects.

Electricity damage comes from the powerful lightning attacks, sometimes the breath weapons of creatures.

Fire damage burns everything in its path and is caused by alchemical formulas and spells.

Sonic damage is usually the result of some magic or unusual effect.

Be aware that armour may only use half of its DR when reducing the damage of these types of energy attack.

Essence is a versatile energy source that can be manipulated for a variety of effects, such as healing, disruption, and necromantic power, depending on the spell, ability, or action being used. Creatures of the Construct type are usually immune to Essence effects.

Force damage is powerful and pure magical energy. Few things can resist this type of damage—not even incorporeal creatures such as ghosts and wraiths.

Be aware that armour is ineffective against these energy types and does not reduce them at all.

PRECISION DAMAGEThere is a special type of damage which is referred to as precision damage. Precision damage is a bonus damage type which is added to another damage type under certain circumstances such as criticals or a Rogues Sneak Attack ability. Precision damage is treated as the original damage type for all rules purposes but may also encounter separate resistances and immunities as detailed in individual abilities. PRECISION DAMAGEThere is a special type of damage which is referred to as precision damage. Precision damage is a bonus damage type which is added to another damage type under certain circumstances such as criticals or a Rogues Sneak Attack ability. Precision damage is treated as the original damage type for all rules purposes but may also encounter separate resistances and immunities as detailed in individual abilities.

ALIGNED DAMAGE

Some weapons and attacks inflict damage which is keyed to a specific aligned trait. Such damage only effects creatures of the opposing trait. So good damage only harms evil creatures, chaos damage effects order creatures etc.

MENTAL DAMAGE

Some damage such as mental is not visible and has no physical form. Mental damage inflicts harm directly to the mind. Armoured targets with no head armour cannot use armour bonuses to DB against mental attacks. Creatures with only a rudimentary or no intelligence (mindless creatures such as constructs) are generally immune to mental damage.

POISON DAMAGE

Poison damage comes in a number of forms and can be delivered by contact, ingestion, injury or inhalation. Some creatures have natural attacks that inflict such damage.

Be aware that armour is ineffective against alignment, mental and poison damage and does not reduce damage at all.

RECURRING DAMAGE

Recurring damage is a condition which inflicts a specified amount of damage each turn. When taking recurring damage, you apply it in Phase 3 of the encounter turn before making a DC 16 flat check to see if the damage ends.

You can attempt to take action to help, stop the recurring damage (GM discretion).

Based upon the action attempted, the GM may deem that your action to stop your recurring damage works automatically or lowers the DC of the Flat-Check.

BLEED DAMAGE

Bleed represents a gradual weakening due to blood loss, pain, and general weariness. When you are suffering from Bleed you lose a certain number of HPs at the end of your turn each round in Phase 3 of the encounter turn, until the Bleed is stopped.

The number of HPs lost due to Bleed from different wounds is cumulative.

For example, if a character is losing 2 HPs each Round, receiving another wound Bleeding for 3 HPs will bring them to lose a total of 5 HPs each Round.

There are four severities of Bleeding, based on the total amount of HPs that you are losing each Round:

• Light Bleeding: You are losing 1 to 4 HPs each Round.

• Moderate Bleeding: You are losing 5 to 8 HPs each Round.

• Severe Bleeding: You are losing 9 to 12 HPs each Round.

• Dire: You are losing 13+ HPs each round.

If you are suffering from light bleeding, you may attempt to remove it in the same way as other recurring damage each round by making a flat check. More serious bleeding must be healed with the Medicine skill or using magic.

SEPARATE WOUNDSFor more realism, you may wish to keep track of bleeding wounds individually. This would allow characters to make a flat check to stop only one bleed (usually the lightest) each turn. This requires more admin but can be much more interesting. SEPARATE WOUNDSFor more realism, you may wish to keep track of bleeding wounds individually. This would allow characters to make a flat check to stop only one bleed (usually the lightest) each turn. This requires more admin but can be much more interesting.

HEALING & CRITICALS

When a Critical Hit inflicts some kind of condition, it is vital to know how or when that condition will be removed. This is listed under the Persistence column on each of the critical tables at the end of this chapter. These are explained in detail here:

Minimal Effect (M) – The injury is a minor annoyance and only lasts until the end of your next turn.

Duration (D) – The injury persists for an amount of time which will be determined by the severity of the critical.

INJURY DURATION

Critical Severity

Duration

Minor

1d4 rounds

Serious

1d6+2 rounds

Deadly

1d10+5 rounds

At the end of this duration, the injuries effect is removed with no further penalty.

Until Healed (UH) – An injury that lasts until healed is removed once the target is magically healed to full HP or is restored to full HP through mundane means and rests for 10 minutes. Other spells may heal such an injury as well.

Full Rest (FR) – An injury that requires full rest cannot be removed until the target has had a minimum of 8 hours sleep. Such injuries may also require other healing to remove as well. Any other specific requirements will be explained in the description.

Permanent (P) – A permanent injury lasts until it is healed in the appropriate manner. This will differ depending upon the Injury. If for example the targets eyes were destroyed, a Restore Sense would not suffice as the eyes would need to be regenerated before sight could be fully returned.

Be aware that these rules only apply to conditions that do not have their own durations (Bleeding, Recurring, sickened etc).

FATAL INJURIES

If a character is subjected to a critical that has the Fatal descriptor in the Severity column, they are on the verge of death. A character suffering from such an injury cannot lose the Dying condition when making a recovery check and therefore cannot be brought above 0 HP. A fatal injury can only be healed once its cause has been removed (usually through magic).

FAST HEALING & REGENERATION

A creature with fast healing or regeneration regains the listed amount of Hit Points each round at the beginning of its turn.

Fast healing and regeneration also affect your ability to heal injuries. Fast Healing reduces your Injured condition by its value every hour. Regenerate does the same, every 10 minutes.

NATURAL HEALING

You recover one tenth of your Total HPs for every full hour of rest in a safe environment, although medicine checks, herbs or magical healing can increase the amount recovered.

INSTANT DEATH

Some effects and criticals can kill you immediately. If an effect states it kills you outright, you die without having to exceed Death State and without being reduced to 0 Hit Points. If this is a critical, it will have the Death descriptor in the severity column.

DEATH & DYING

If you are reduced to 0 HP or lower by an attack the following process occurs immediately:

• Your HP becomes 0 (do not track negative HP while dying).

• You gain Unconscious and Dying 1.

• If the effect that reduced you to 0 HP was a critical hit (or similarly lethal at GM discretion), you gain Dying 2 instead.

Massive Damage (Instant Death): If a single instance of damage would reduce you to 0 HP and the excess damage (beyond what it took to reach 0) is equal to or greater than your maximum HP, you die immediately.

DYING CHECK

At the start of Phase 1 of each of your turns while you have the Dying condition, attempt a Level-Based Fortitude Saving Throw.

Apply the result:

Critical Reduce Dying by 2.

Success Reduce Dying by 1.

Partial No change.

Chaos Treat as a Modified Result and the GM introduces a minor complication or benefit (no additional mechanics required).

Failure Increase Dying by 1.

Fumble Increase Dying by 2.

Blunder The lights go out, and you are off to meet the big fella in the sky or the grim chap with the scythe, you have expired.

If your Dying condition is reduced to 0, you lose the Dying condition (see Recovery).

TAKING DAMAGE WHILE DYING

While you have the Dying condition, you are already at 0 HP. Damage does not reduce HP; it worsens your condition.

• If you take damage increase Dying by 1.

• If the damage instance is from a critical hit (or similarly brutal effect at GM discretion), increase Dying by 2 instead.

If your Dying condition value exceeds your Death State attribute, you die.

RECOVERY: LOSING THE DYING CONDITION

When your Dying condition value is reduced to 0, the following happens:

• You lose the Dying condition.

• You remain at 0 HP and Unconscious unless you are brought to 1+ HP, in which case you lose the Unconscious condition.

• Your Fatigued condition increases by 1.

HEALING WHILE DYING

Healing affects a character with the Dying condition differently to a character who is able and moving. If a character receives the benefit of a magical effect (including regeneration) that heals HP while they have the Dying condition, the condition is reduced by 1. Non-magical healing (including fast healing) has no effect on you unless the Resuscitation (Medicine) action is used.

The Resuscitation action is detailed on page 85.

INJURIES

Injuries are long-lasting wounds, like broken bones or torn muscles, that severely impede your activity.

They’re represented by the dazed, injured and weakened conditions.

Injuries are categorized into three severities, according to their value.

• Injuries with a value of up to 4 are called Minor Injuries.

• Injuries with a value from 5-7 are considered Serious Injuries.

• Injuries with a value of 8+ are considered to be Deadly Injuries.

Each Injury must be recorded and healed separately, but the penalties they inflict stack.

INCAPACITATION FROM INJURIES

If your combined value of Injuries reaches a total of 10 or more, you gain the Unconscious Condition until your penalties are reduced to 10 or less.

This can be from any combination of penalties. A PC can only withstand so much pain and trauma so if you are suffering from combined penalties (from any source) equal to 20 or more, this comes into play immediately.

TREATING INJURIES

Injuries need time, care, and rest to heal. Injured characters can travel at a slow pace or engage in similarly light activities, but fighting or exerting themselves will prevent any recovery for that day.

Minor Injuries will heal by themselves in three days of rest. No Check is required for these injuries, but a DC 20 Medicine Skill Check and the usage of a Healer’s Kit will halve their recovery time.

Other Injuries require a Medicine Skill Check and the use of a Healer’s Kit to start healing. Once the recovery process is started, as long as the patient keeps resting, Light and Serious Injuries will slowly turn into less severe Injuries, until they’re fully healed.

A Serious Injury requires a DC 24 Medicine Check and will turn into a Minor Injury (lowering value accordingly) in 10 days of rest, after being treated.

Deadly Injuries start healing with a successful DC 30 Medicine Check and will become a Serious Injury (lowering value accordingly) after 20 days if treated. Once turned into Minor Injuries, Serious Injuries will continue to heal without the need of any further treatment, as long as the character rests.

Fatal and Death Injuries will not heal without magical aid.

DEATH & DISMEMBERMENTDead characters cannot be healed by normal means; only a miracle or the strongest of magic can bring them back into play.Magical healing is also the only way to repair destroyed organs or severed limbs.If you are missing an eye, you will suffer a -4 penalty to all Perception Checks which rely on the sense of sight, and a -4 penalty to all ranged Attack Checks.If you lose a hand or arm you won’t be able to wield two-handed weapons and suffer a -4 penalty for tasks requiring the use of both hands.If you are missing a foot or leg you move at half your normal Speed, cannot add your Dexterity to your DB and suffer a -5 penalty to all Movement Actions.DEATH & DISMEMBERMENTDead characters cannot be healed by normal means; only a miracle or the strongest of magic can bring them back into play.Magical healing is also the only way to repair destroyed organs or severed limbs.If you are missing an eye, you will suffer a -4 penalty to all Perception Checks which rely on the sense of sight, and a -4 penalty to all ranged Attack Checks.If you lose a hand or arm you won’t be able to wield two-handed weapons and suffer a -4 penalty for tasks requiring the use of both hands.If you are missing a foot or leg you move at half your normal Speed, cannot add your Dexterity to your DB and suffer a -5 penalty to all Movement Actions.

EXHAUSTION

Your character will often carry out physically strenuous activity for long periods of time and run the risk of becoming tired. When your character has been carrying out such activities for a determined period, they must make an Exhaustion Check.

EXHAUSTION CHECK

An exhaustion check is an easy (DC -2) level-based Fortitude saving throw with the following results.

Critical You can do this all day and gain a +2-circumstance bonus to any further exhaustion checks made within the next ten minutes.

Success You are fine for now and incur no fatigue because of your activity.

Partial This is hard work; you gain 1 fatigue.

Failure This is just so damn tiring; you gain 2 fatigue.

Fumble You never knew that this activity could drain you so much, you gain 4 fatigue.

Blunder The exertion is just all too much; you gain 8 fatigue.

Your GM may allow you to make certain exhaustion checks such as sustaining a spell by using a will save instead of fortitude under certain circumstances.Your GM may allow you to make certain exhaustion checks such as sustaining a spell by using a will save instead of fortitude under certain circumstances.

SAVING THROWS

Some attacks and abilities require you to make a Saving Throw (ST) to avoid or reduce their effect.

There are three types of saving throw as detailed below.

FORTITUDE SAVING THROW

This saving throw is used to resist effects that target your body or health. To determine your Fortitude Save you use the following formula:

Con + Class Bonus + Other Bonus

REFLEX SAVING THROW

This saving throw is used to dodge area attacks and unexpected situations. To determine your Reflex Save you use the following formula:

Dex + Class Bonus + Other Bonus

Be aware that your character must have room to move out of the way of an area attack that provokes a reflex save and must be able to move. If this is not the case, the GM will apply penalties.

WILL SAVING THROW

This saving throw is used to resist magical and mental effects. To determine your Will Save you use the following formula:

Wis + Class Bonus + Other Bonus

RESOLVING SAVING THROWS

When a Saving Throw is called for, you must make an Open-Ended Roll and add your relevant Saving Throw Bonus, plus any applicable modifier.

If the result is equal to or higher than the Save DC you manage to resist the effects of the attack.

Sometimes, the amount by which you fail the saving throw might affect the outcome. As a general rule, if you succeed by 10 or more, it usually results in a Critical success (Critical). If you fail by 10 or more the result is usually a Fumble. Specifics of saving throw failure results are detailed in each spell, skill or ability.

SAVING THROW DIFFICULTY

Referred to as a Save DC, this is the amount which you must equal or exceed to gain a success on the saving throw check. The Save DC is usually the level of the effect with potential modifiers.

OTHER MODIFIERS

Each saving throw may have a number of modifiers which could affect its Save DC further. Spells and magic also have their own modifiers and some additional rules when dealing with saving throws which are discussed in more detail in Chapter 8.

MOVEMENT

You may use AP during an encounter to take actions which have the move trait. The move actions available to you are based upon your skills, abilities and feats, although most characters can carry out the basic move actions (see chapter 4).

Sometimes movement can become more difficult based upon terrain or other factors.

GRID MOVEMENT

It can be easier to track the movement and relative positions of characters by using a battle grid or mat. Using a battle grid allows you to accurately track the positions of all combatants and removes positional confusion that may arise otherwise.

Each square grid on a battle grid represents 5 feet across in the game world. This means that if your character moves in a straight line you use 5 feet of movement for every square.

DIAGONAL MOVEMENT

Because diagonal movement covers more ground, it is counted differently. The first diagonal square you move during your turn costs 5 feet, the second costs 10 feet, and each additional diagonal square continues to alternate between 5 feet and 10 feet. For example, moving 4 squares diagonally costs 5, then 10, then 5, then 10 feet, for a total of 30 feet. Track this diagonal count across all movement you make during your turn, then reset it at the end of your turn.

TERRAIN

The battlefield is not always a pristine and open expanse; it is often dotted with various terrain features that can impact movement and manoeuvrability. When engaged in an encounter, the environment around you becomes a crucial element to consider.

Detailed below are the main considerations to consider from a terrain perspective.

DIFFICULT TERRAIN

Portions of the battlefield may be covered in difficult terrain, such as muddy swamps, thick undergrowth, or deep snow. Moving through these areas’ costs x2 the usual amount of movement.

Malisha moves through an area of difficult terrain which is 20 feet across, it costs her 40 feet of movement instead of 20 feet.

FORMIDABLE TERRAIN

The battlefield may be covered in thick vines, be extremely marshy underfoot or be at a gradient that does not require a climb check but still slows you down.

Moving through these areas’ costs x3 the usual amount of movement.

Be aware that you cannot Step into difficult or formidable terrain.

Be aware that if you have a Fly speed, you are unhindered by difficult terrain.

HAZARDOUS TERRAIN

Traversing hazardous terrain poses a significant risk as it can inflict damage upon you as you move through it. The extent of this damage varies depending on the specific type of hazardous terrain encountered. It's important to note that hazardous terrain may also overlap with any of the other terrain here.

UNUSUAL SURFACES

Various surface types may require you to make a skill check when traversing them. Narrow surfaces or uneven ground may require a Balance (Acrobatics) check to maintain stability and prevent you from falling. Furthermore, if you are struck by an attack while on such a surface, the GM may require you to make a similar check to avoid losing your footing.

Whilst moving on any unusual surface, you are flat-footed.

OBJECTS

While it would be ideal to have a spacious and uncluttered area for simplicity's sake, such circumstances are seldom encountered. During an encounter, you are likely to encounter various obstacles such as statues, chests, low walls, and other objects that may impede your movement. How an object effects your ability to move is usually determined by the GM based upon its size and dimensions.

TRG is not completely dependent on a battle grid, but the examples used in this chapter work with a Square 5 x 5-foot grid. It is possible to adapt all these rules to other types of battle grids (such as hex grids) but these rules do not cover this.TRG is not completely dependent on a battle grid, but the examples used in this chapter work with a Square 5 x 5-foot grid. It is possible to adapt all these rules to other types of battle grids (such as hex grids) but these rules do not cover this.

FORCED MOVEMENTWhen an external force compels you to move or if you find yourself falling, the distance of your movement is determined by the effect that initiated it, disregarding your Speed. Since this movement is not initiated by you, it does not trigger reactions that are typically triggered by voluntary movement.In situations where forced movement would lead you to occupy a space that is inaccessible, whether due to obstacles obstructing your path or the lack of a required movement type, you cease moving in the last available space you can occupy. The path taken during forced movement is usually chosen by the entity or effect responsible for the forced movement. If you are pushed or pulled, it is possible to be moved through hazardous terrain or even pushed off ledges, unless specific abilities or conditions prevent such actions. However, abilities that reposition you in alternative ways are unable to place you in hazardous locations, unless expressly stated otherwise. In instances where uncertainty arises regarding the permissibility of forced movement, the GM has the final say.FORCED MOVEMENTWhen an external force compels you to move or if you find yourself falling, the distance of your movement is determined by the effect that initiated it, disregarding your Speed. Since this movement is not initiated by you, it does not trigger reactions that are typically triggered by voluntary movement.In situations where forced movement would lead you to occupy a space that is inaccessible, whether due to obstacles obstructing your path or the lack of a required movement type, you cease moving in the last available space you can occupy. The path taken during forced movement is usually chosen by the entity or effect responsible for the forced movement. If you are pushed or pulled, it is possible to be moved through hazardous terrain or even pushed off ledges, unless specific abilities or conditions prevent such actions. However, abilities that reposition you in alternative ways are unable to place you in hazardous locations, unless expressly stated otherwise. In instances where uncertainty arises regarding the permissibility of forced movement, the GM has the final say.

SIZE, SPACE & REACH

The size of a creature determines how much space it occupies and what kind of reach it possesses in melee.

If a creature has an attack form which is longer than its usual size (such as a reach attack or weapon) then it is possible for any of its targets to attack the reached appendage. Against a creature this will allow an attack against the body part. If reach is being gained from a weapon, then only actions which effect that weapon (such as disarm) may be used against it.

Be aware that to make an attack against a body part or weapon which is attacking at reach, you must use the Ready Action and strike it when it attacks you.

A creature with a size of small or greater occupies at least one square on the grid. Tiny & Diminutive creatures can occupy the same space as another creature and must do so to make attacks against them. Up to four Tiny creatures can occupy the same space and up to eight Diminutive creatures.

SIZE MODIFIERS

Creatures which are larger than medium have a reach which is naturally greater than smaller creatures and also occupy more space on the map.

SIZES & THE GRID

Creatures of different sizes occupy different amounts of space on the battle grid and can threaten a different area with their attacks. A creature’s space is the number of squares it fills; Small and Medium creatures typically occupy 1 square, while larger creatures may occupy multiple squares and must follow the normal rules for fitting, squeezing, and positioning on the grid. A creature’s reach is how far it can make melee attacks and threaten squares around it; most Small and Medium creatures have a reach of 5 feet, while Large and larger creatures often have a longer reach, allowing them to strike and threaten squares farther away. Space determines where a creature can stand and move, while reach determines which squares it can attack and control. Below are specific examples for each size of creature.

A Diminutive or Tiny creature has a reach of 0 feet and must occupy a targets square to attack them. A tiny creature does not need to make checks to occupy a targets square but is subject to reactions as normal.

A Small or Medium creature has a reach of 5 feet and may attack any creature that is adjacent to them. Such a creature occupies one square on a battle grid.

A Large creature has a reach of 10 feet and may attack any creature that is within this reach which is measured from any square it occupies. Such a creature occupies four squares on a battle grid

A Huge creature has a reach of 15 feet and may attack any creature that is within this reach which is measured from any square it occupies. Such a creature occupies nine squares on a battle grid

A Gargantuan creature has a reach of 20 feet and may attack any creature that is within this reach which is measured from any square it occupies. Such a creature occupies sixteen squares on a battle grid.

A Colossal creature has a reach of 25 feet and may attack any creature that is within this reach which is measured from any square it occupies. Such a creature occupies twenty-five squares on a battle grid.

MOVING THROUGH A CREATURE’S SPACE

You may move through the occupied space of a willing ally. However, when it comes to moving through an unwilling creature's space, you must make a Tumble (Acrobatics) check. It is important to note that you cannot end your turn in a space already occupied by another creature, although you can temporarily occupy their space during a move action. If two creatures accidentally occupy the same square, the GM has the authority to determine which one is displaced from the square or if either of them falls prone.

REALISTIC METHODOLOGYYour GM may decide that moving freely through allied spaces is a little unrealistic. In this case, the GM may ask an ally to make a Free (0 AP) Perception check to have the awareness that you are attempting to move past them, with a failure preventing your movement.REALISTIC METHODOLOGYYour GM may decide that moving freely through allied spaces is a little unrealistic. In this case, the GM may ask an ally to make a Free (0 AP) Perception check to have the awareness that you are attempting to move past them, with a failure preventing your movement.

PRONE CREATURES

If a creature is prone and is your size or smaller, then you can occupy its space, such a space is treated as difficult terrain.

It is more difficult to move through the space of a prone creature that is larger than you. Such spaces would be treated as Greater difficult terrain but may require climb checks to traverse safely.

It is impossible for a prone creature to stand up while someone else occupies its space, but it can Crawl to a space where it’s able to stand, or it can attempt to Shove the other creature out of the way.

SIZE CONSIDERATIONS

If a creature is at least three sizes larger than you, then you can freely move through its space. Furthermore, this also works in reverse as a creature can also move through the space of a creature which is three sizes smaller. You still cannot end your movement in the space of another creature unless you are Tiny or Diminutive.

Be aware that even though you may be able to freely move through a creature’s square without a Tumble (Acrobatics) check, you still may provoke reactions for doing so.

COVER

It is possible to use your surroundings to grant yourself a bonus to DB and Reflex saving throws, this is called being in cover.

Standard cover provides a +4-circumstance bonus to your DB, Reflex saves and Hide & Sneak (Stealth) checks. However, you also have the option to enhance your cover further using the Take Cover basic action. By employing this action, you can upgrade your cover to greater cover, resulting in a heightened circumstance bonus of +8.

In cases where cover is more minimal or provided by a creature, such as when using another creature as cover, you are considered to have lesser cover. While lesser cover still offers some protection, it provides a slightly reduced circumstance bonus of +2 to your DB.

Be aware that a creature with standard or greater cover can attempt to use Stealth to Hide, but lesser cover isn't insufficient for this action.

COVER TABLE

Type of Cover

Bonus

Can Hide

Lesser

+2

No

Standard

+4

Yes

Greater

+8

Yes

Cover is relative, so you might simultaneously have cover against one creature and not another. Cover applies only if your path to the target is partially blocked. If a creature is entirely behind a wall or the like, you don't have line of effect and typically can't target it at all.

The GM will make a final decision as to whether you or an opponent has cover against an attack.

REACTIONS

Your reactions allow you to act in response to another action. You cannot usually use a reaction before your first turn in an encounter, but the GM may determine that such a thing is possible under certain circumstances.

As soon as your turn begins, you gain your 3 AP and your reaction. You may only use one reaction per round although some abilities or feats may allow you to use more reactions in a round.

Be aware that it impossible to use a reaction if you have no awareness of the reactions trigger.

Reactions are vitally important during an encounter, and it is essential that you keep a track of which reactions are available to you. All PCs’ (although not necessarily all NPCs’) have access to the Attack of Opportunity reaction.

Be aware that it is usually impossible to use a reaction in response to another reaction. Your GM may deem that sometimes this is possible under certain circumstances.

TRIGGERING REACTIONS

Some reactions and free actions are triggered by a creature using an action with the move trait. The most notable example is Attack of Opportunity. Actions with the move trait can trigger reactions or free actions throughout the course of the distance travelled. Each time you exit a hex (or move 5 feet if not using a grid) within a creature’s reach, your movement triggers those reactions and free actions (although no more than once per move action for a given reacting creature). If you use a move action but don’t move out of a hex, the trigger instead happens at the end of that action or ability.

Some actions, such as Step, specifically state they don’t trigger reactions or free actions based on movement.

With his last action Signus stepped away from the Ogre. Unfortunately for Signus, the Ogre has a Reach of 10-feet so if he now takes a move action or any other action that provokes a reaction, then the Ogre may well strike him with an Attack of Opportunity (if it can).

RANGED ATTACKS

Ranged attacks allow you to hit targets from a distance. Attacks made with missile or thrown weapons, as well as those made with certain spells, are all considered to be ranged attacks.

To be able to make a ranged attack you must have a clear line of sight to your target. Additionally, the target must be within the attack range of your weapon or spell.

LINE OF SIGHT

You have line of sight to a target if you can clearly see at least part of it. See Cover later in the chapter for more information about partially hidden targets.

In the above image, Jonas cannot attack the Ogre using his shortbow as he has no line of sight (the wall is in the way).

ATTACK RANGE

Ranged and thrown weapons each have a listed range increment, and attacks with them grow less accurate against targets farther away. If your target is at or within the listed range increment, also called the first range increment, you take no penalty to the attack roll. If you’re attacking beyond that range increment, you take a –4 penalty for each additional increment beyond the first. You can attempt to attack with a ranged weapon or thrown weapon up to six range increments away, but the farther away you are, the harder it is to hit your target.

Spell attacks use their own rules for attack range (see Chapter 8 – Magic).

RANGED ATTACKS IN MELEE

Normally, your ranged attacks are directed against distant foes, but there are occasions in which you may be forced to use a ranged weapon or Spell while Engaged in melee. In these cases, apply the following rules:

• Engaged characters suffer a -4 penalty to all their ranged attack rolls

• Making a ranged attack whilst engaged provokes reactions.

FIRING INTO MELEE

If you are engaged in melee, you have standard cover (+4 circumstance DB) against all ranged attacks aimed at you.

When making a ranged attack into melee, if your attack misses by an amount between 1-4 you have chance of hitting one of the other combatants. If there is only one other creature involved in the melee, then that is the target that is hit, roll damage as normal although this attack cannot result in a critical injury.

If there are multiple additional targets in the melee, each rolls a d20 and the on with the lowest result is hit by the attack.

Jonas is making a ranged Strike with his shortbow in an attempt to kill the Ogre that is currently battling with his companions. Jonas has line of sight but due to the Ogre being involved in melee, it gains a +4-circumstance bonus to DB against the attack.

FLANKING

When making a melee attack against a creature, it is possible to gain a +2-circumstance bonus to your attack based upon your position in relation to any allies who are fighting the same creature.

Flanking occurs when two or more characters are positioned on opposite sides of an enemy, effectively surrounding them or attacking from multiple directions.

To be considered flanking, the characters or creatures must occupy squares that are adjacent to the enemy in a way that forms a straight line. This line can be horizontal, vertical, or diagonal, if the squares are contiguous and form a direct path of attack. The flanking characters must also be threatening the same enemy, meaning they are capable of making melee attacks against that enemy.

FLANK EXAMPLE 2FLANK EXAMPLE 2FLANK EXAMPLE 1FLANK EXAMPLE 1

Jonas and Signus both gain a flank bonus in flank example 1 as they are fighting a medium creature and are at opposite sides of that opponent. In flank example 2, they do not get the flank bonus as they are adjacent.

To flank a large (or bigger) creature, two or more characters must be positioned on opposite sides of the creature, just like flanking a regular-sized creature. However, since a large creature occupies multiple squares, the flanking characters must be adjacent to any of the squares occupied by the large creature to establish a flanking position.

FLANK EXAMPLE 4FLANK EXAMPLE 4FLANK EXAMPLE 3FLANK EXAMPLE 3

Jonas and Signus both gain a flank bonus in flank example 3 as they are fighting a large creature and are on opposite sides of that creature. In flank example 4, they do not get the flank bonus as they are not on opposite sides.

Furthermore, you and an ally must also meet the following conditions:

• Capability to Act: Both be able to take actions during the current turn, ensuring that neither of you is incapacitated or unable to act.

• Melee Weapons or Unarmed Attack: Both be wielding melee weapons or possess the ability to make lethal unarmed attacks.

• Unimpeded Attack Ability: You cannot have any conditions that hinder or prevent you from initiating attacks (such as confused or fleeing).

• Reach to the Enemy: Both must have the enemy within your respective reach. This means that the target must be within striking distance of your melee weapons or unarmed attack range, allowing you to effectively coordinate your assault.

MOUNTED COMBAT

Mounted combat introduces an exciting dynamic to encounters, allowing you to engage in battles while mounted on various creatures or vehicles.

Mounted combat involves you utilizing mounts, such as horses, giant eagles, or fantastical creatures, as a means of transportation and as formidable assets in combat.

MOUNTED CHARACTERS

Certain creatures can serve as mounts, allowing you to ride them into combat. As explained in the Mount (Handle Animal) action, it is necessary for your mount to be at least one size larger than you and willing to be ridden. During combat, your mount acts based on your initiative. To direct your mount's actions, you must use the Command an Animal (Handle Animal) action. Failure to do so will result in the animal acting according to its own natural instincts and behaviours.

MOUNTED ATTACKS

While mounted, you and your mount are regarded as single entity for the following circumstances:

• Shared AP: You and your mount operate with a combined pool of action points, which is determined by the character with the lowest amount of action points between you. This means that you must coordinate your actions and strategize together, effectively sharing resources to maximize your combat effectiveness.

Tomas is riding his warhorse into combat and has already used 1 AP to command an animal. He and his mount now have 2 AP remaining between them to use for the remainder of their turn.

• Shared Multiple Attack Penalty: When making multiple attacks in a single turn, both you and your mount are subject to the same multiple attack penalty. This penalty ensures that successive attacks become progressively more difficult to execute. By sharing this penalty, it reinforces the need for coordination and synchronization between you and your mount when executing multiple strikes.

• Shared Space: When mounted, you occupy all the squares within your mount's space when making your attacks.

If you are a Medium-sized rider on a Large mount, you can attack a creature with a reach of 10 feet rather than 5 feet (assuming of course that your mount does not have reduced reach).

Finally, you gain a +2-circumstance bonus to all attack checks against unmounted targets whilst mounted. This bonus reflects the increased effectiveness of your attacks against opponents who lack the mobility and advantage of being mounted.

MOUNTED DEFENCE

When you are mounted, potential attackers have the option to target either you or your mount. This means that any effects or abilities that affect multiple creatures, will impact both of you within the affected area.

You are considered to be within an attacker's reach or range if any square occupied by your mount falls within their reach or range. Since your mount is larger than you and you share its space, you have lesser cover against attacks targeting you when you’re mounted if the mount would be in the way.

AERIAL COMBAT

There will almost certainly be occasions when your combat will take to the sky using various means, such as innate abilities, spells, or enchanted items. However, the act of flying requires conscious effort, as flying creatures must use the Fly action to navigate through the air. Engaging in more challenging manoeuvres, like abruptly changing direction by 180 degrees or attempting to pass through narrow openings, may require the use of the Aerial Manoeuvre (Acrobatics) action.

It is important to note that flying creatures, like any other, are subject to the laws of gravity and can potentially fall from the sky. In such instances, the rules for falling would come into play, accounting for the distance fallen and any associated consequences.

The GM makes the final decision as to whether certain actions that are typically performed on the ground would be feasible or effective in the air. For instance, a flying creature would face limitations when it comes to executing a Jump (Athletics) action, as the mechanics of jumping rely upon solid ground for propulsion.

UNDERWATER COMBAT

Sometimes you will yourself having to fight and battle with your enemies in an aquatic environment. When such a situation occurs, the following rules are used:

• You’re flat-footed when fighting or moving in the water unless you have a swim Speed.

• You gain acid and fire resistance.

• You take a –2 circumstance penalty to melee slashing or bludgeoning attacks that pass-through water.

• Ranged attacks that deal bludgeoning or slashing damage automatically miss if the attacker or target is underwater, and piercing ranged attacks made by an underwater creature or against an underwater target have their range increments halved.

• Any attempt to use a fire spell underwater results in a failure. Furthermore, actions with the fire trait also fail automatically.

• Any spells or electricity abilities used underwater immediately have radius equal to the normal range of the spell emanating from their originator or caster. The creator of such an effect always takes double damage from the effect.

• Some ground-based actions might not work underwater or while floating (GM discretion).

DROWNING & SUFFOCATION

You can hold your breath for a number of rounds equal to 5 + Con or 1 round whichever is greater.

Reduce your remaining air by 1 round at the end of each of your turns, or by 2 if you attacked or cast any spells that turn. You also lose 1 round worth of air each time you are critically hit or critically fail a save against a damaging effect. If you speak (including casting spells with verbal components or activating items with command components) you lose all remaining air.

When you run out of air, you fall unconscious and start suffocating. You can’t recover from being unconscious and must attempt a Fortitude save, needing to achieve 20 or greater, at the end of each of your turns. On a failure, you take 10 damage (untyped), and on a critical failure, you die. On each check after the first, you take a cumulative -2 penalty to the save and the damage increases by 5; these increases are cumulative. Once your access to air is restored, you stop suffocating and are no longer unconscious.

Be aware that you only regain consciousness if there are no other factors causing the condition.

CRITICAL HITS & INJURIES

The final part of this chapter contains all the rules for critical hits and critical injuries. This includes the critical injury tables and fumble tables that are needed in combat. The first tables in this section are the critical injury tables.

CRITICAL INJURY

One of the most effective ways to leave a lasting impression in a fight is to leave your opponent with a little something to remember you by. Critical injuries offer an opportunity for you (and the bad guys) to scar, break, maim and even kill the enemy, brutally establishing your battle superiority.

When making an attack, if your AV is 5 or greater, then you have inflicted a critical hit.

Your total AV determines the severity of the critical hit and how much additional damage is inflicted because of it.

Critical Severity: This is the Critical Severity which determines how your d100 is rolled on the critical table and how much additional damage you inflict.

Dice Mod: Your critical roll is either made at disadvantage, normal or with advantage.

Bonus Damage: A critical hit adds bonus damage of your primary damage type (after BAB modification). This damage is precision damage in type.

Tharngar strikes a sneaky Ogre and inflicts a critical with a severity of serious. Tharngar is currently inflicting 1d8 base damage (2d8 total) with his Warhammer. His critical therefore inflicts an additional 2d8 damage.

DAMAGE REDUCTION & CRITICALS

If you take a critical injury from an attack, your DR to lower the damage of that attack is only applicable if you have armour coverage for the area struck (as determined by the critical injury result).

Valgar is wearing Plate armour which only covers the torso granting him DR 6. He is struck for a critical hit which hits him in the leg. The total damage inflicted by the critical hit is 14. This damage is not lowered as Valgar has no leg armour. If the attack had not inflicted a critical, or the critical roll had indicated a torso hit, Valgar would have been able to use his armour to reduce the damage from 14 to 8.

CRITICAL SEVERITY

If you inflict a critical it will have one of the following three severities. The severity of the critical determines several factors as detailed below.

MINOR

A minor critical is the least damaging type of Critical Strike, often associated with small scratches and bruises. A minor critical is rolled with disadvantage (d100 taking the lower number as the tens die).

SERIOUS

A serious critical is no laughing matter. They can easily maim, stun, or inflict bleeding and put the target at a severe disadvantage, tearing it down very quickly. A serious critical is rolled as a normal d100 roll

DEADLY

A deadly critical is something you want to avoid, but to lavish upon your opponents. A deadly critical is rolled with advantage (d100 taking the higher number as the tens die).

INJURY DC

Some effects of a critical may require the target to make a Saving Throw to avoid a more serious effect. When required, the Injury DC used is that of the attacking creatures Attack DC (attack bonus +10). This may be modified by feats or other abilities.

CRITICAL RESISTANCE

A creature with critical resistance has great physical stamina and is harder to inflict critical hits upon. A creatures Critical Resistance (CR) increases the AV required by an incoming attack to inflict a critical.

So, a creature with CR 1 would take a minor critical if the AV was 6 or higher a serious if it was 16 or higher and so forth.

CRITICAL IMMUNITY

A creature or character with critical immunity ignores all critical injuries.

ARMOUR GRANTS CR

To make armoured characters a little sturdier, you may grant them CR. When using this rule, a character wearing medium armour has CR 1 and heavy armour CR 2.

It also important to note that when using this rule, if an attack targets a specific part of the body (ambush, vital strike), then CR is bypassed if no armour is worn at that location.

CRITICAL INJURY RESULT

If an injury is inflicted, roll a d100 based upon the severity on the appropriate critical table to determine its effect.

PERSISTENCE

This column determines how long the injury will last. These are explained in more detail on page 195.

(M) Minimal Effect; (D) Duration; (UH) Until Healed

(FR) Full Rest; (P) Permanent.

This column may also have the Death or Fatal descriptor (see below).

INJURY EFFECT

This determines the outcome of the critical and all effects are applied immediately.

Armoured

Some critical results will be modified if the target is wearing armour. If this is the case, the effect will have an “Armoured:” entry. When this is the case, use the instructions given to either replace the critical effects or modify them.

Graze to shoulder Injured 1. Armoured: Weakened 1.

So, with the above critical result, if the target is wearing armour they will be Weakened 1 instead of Injured 1.

Be Aware that if our armour reduces the effect of a critical result, it also takes damage as detailed in Chapter 6.

DEATH OR FATAL

If a critical result has the Death or Fatal descriptors, then the target may make a Fortitude (Will against Mental) saving throw against the Injury DC (see above) with a Hard (DC +2) for Fatal and a Very Hard (DC +5) for Death, to avoid the effect. If the saving throw is successful, the result of the critical is lowered by 10 and the new result applied. Furthermore, any such critical effect always reduces you to 0 HP.

Be Aware that no additional saving throw may be made if the new result also has one of these traits.

CHAOS RESULT

When making the critical injury roll, if a an unmodified 66 is rolled, chaos trigger. When this happens, replace the critical injury result with the following:

Get ready for random, roll 1d30+70 and use as the result of the injury. You must make a roll on the appropriate fumble table and regain 1 conviction. If you roll a 1 on the fumble, you are also subjected to your critical result.

QUICK DAMAGE

To speed up the game, you may wish to add extra dice of damage as static damage as well. If this is the case, please use the below table to apply extra damage in place of dice.

MODES OF LETHALITY

You may adjust the lethality of criticals to suit your groups needs very easily. If you want to have less lethality and have criticals occur less often, simply increase the AV required to inflict criticals. If you want the game to be more lethal, you may decrease the AV required to inflict criticals.

SPECIFIC LOCATION INJURIES

You may feel that the injured condition and the penalties which you take from this condition are a little too generic and severe. If this is the case then feel free to apply the penalty received from the injured condition to specific actions carried out that are appropriate to the injury only (speed for legs, attacks and climbing for arms etc).

Using the injured condition in this way requires a little more administration but adds a level of realism to the game.

WADE THROUGH THE MOOKS

Managing numerous minor NPCs with injuries and penalties can quickly become overwhelming for a GM and disrupt the flow of gameplay. To simplify this, the Wade Through the Mooks rule adjusts how PCs handle critical hits against Minor Creatures.

When a PC lands a critical hit on a Minor Creature, they inflict additional hit point damage and apply the Injured condition to the target as the hits decrease to represent them taking injuries.

DETERMINING INJURY & PENALTIES

Minor Creatures also experience penalties based on their remaining hit points, reflected by their Wound Threshold. These penalties apply to attack rolls, defence checks, and other relevant actions:

A minor creature, referred to as a MNPC (Mook Non-Player Character), is usually one that is at least four levels lower than the average party level.

FUMBLES

This mechanic introduces a chance for a weapon or attack to fumble (make a critical mistake) when rolling an Unmodified 1 (UM 1) on a d20 attack check. Here’s how it works step by step:

Unmodified 1 on an Attack Roll:

If the result of the d20 roll for your attack is a natural 1 (without modifiers), this triggers the possibility of a fumble.

Fumble Check:

To determine if the attack results in an actual fumble, you roll a second d20 (called the Fumble Check) against the weapon's or attack's Fumble DC.

The Fumble DC represents how likely the weapon or attack is to fumble. For example, a poorly balanced or fragile weapon might have a higher Fumble DC, making it more prone to fumbling. Conversely, a well-crafted or stable weapon could have a lower Fumble DC, making fumbling less likely.

Outcome of the Fumble Check:

If the Fumble Check meets or exceeds the Fumble DC: The attack narrowly avoids disaster, and no fumble occurs. The result is treated as a simple miss.

If the Fumble Check is below the Fumble DC: The weapon or attack fumbles which triggers a d100 roll on the associated attack fumble table: melee, missile, thrown or unarmed.

The fumble tables are presented in full at the end of this chapter.

In the borderlands of Halmyr, where the wind howls through broken watchtowers and goblins raid under cover of dusk, there lived a warrior named Jarabar. Tall, broad-shouldered, and well-armoured, he looked like a hero of song. But fate, it seems, had a crueller tune for him.

Jarabar was known not for his victories, but for his fumbles—a word uttered with such frequency in his presence it might as well have been a surname.

There was the time he charged a bandit lord, let loose a war cry that echoed down the valley—and promptly flung his sword behind him, striking a goat and starting a minor stampede.

In a duel with a dark knight on the Bridge of Stone, Jarabar drew his blade with too much enthusiasm, lost his grip, and sent the weapon pinwheeling into the river below. He still won the fight—but only because the knight laughed so hard he slipped and fell off the bridge.

But perhaps the most legendary of his mishaps was the Battle of Thornhill. The townsfolk, beset by trolls, pleaded for aid. Jarabar stood atop a barrel, brandishing his axe with righteous fury. He leapt down to face the beasts—and embedded the axe in the ground. Not the troll. The ground. He then attempted to draw his dagger, only to toss it straight into a tree. His boot knife? Lost somewhere in his greaves. The trolls, baffled, simply backed away—convinced they were witnessing some unhinged berserker ritual. They never returned.

Despite it all, Jarabar remained cheerful. He trained harder, practiced daily, and even tied straps around his weapons. None of it helped.

“Maybe,” said the village elder once, watching Jarabar disarm himself by sneezing too hard, “the gods have a different destiny for him.”

And maybe they did. For in a strange twist of irony, it was Jarabar’s unpredictable fumbling that often saved lives—confusing foes, drawing attacks meant for others, or causing the most improbable accidents to land just in his favour.

They say now that when trouble brews in Halmyr, people still call for Jarabar. Not because he’ll win cleanly. But because somehow, impossibly, he always survives, and things somehow work out—if not as planned, then as fumbled.

And so the legend grows: Jarabar the Fumbling Warrior, bane of bandits, slayer of goblins, conqueror of chaos—if only by accident.

You strain a muscle as you make your attack. You take 2 damage.

11-13

Such is your confidence that you overextend and are slightly off balance. You may use no Reactions until the end of your next turn.

14-15

Such is your confidence that you overextend and are slightly off balance. You may use no Reactions until the end of your next turn.

16-20

Your attack is badly executed, and it throws you off balance. You are Weakened 1 until the beginning of your next turn.

21-25

Your clever spin seems impressive but achieves very little. You Trigger Reactions.

26-29

Your attempt to do a star jump does not go unnoticed. You strain something for your efforts and take 1d8 damage.

30

Your attempt to do a star jump does not go unnoticed. You strain something for your efforts and take 1d10 damage.

31-35

You suddenly develop a nasty cramp in your leg. You are Stunned 1.

36-40

The attack looks very impressive but leaves you very exposed. You are Stunned 1 and Flat-Footed until the end of your next turn.

41-45

As you attack, you feel a nasty twinge in your shoulder, that feels like a pulled muscle. You are Weakened 1 until healed.

46-50

You twist and turn and promptly throw up on your boots. Must have been something you ate. You are Sickened 2.

51-55

You did not intend to throw yourself forward like that. You have strained something in the process. You are Injured 1 until healed.

56-60

There is something wrong with one of your legs, and it distracts you enough to miss with your attack. You are Slowed 1 until healed.

61-65

You often have great ideas when in combat, but not this time. Headbutting your target ends badly. You inflict 5 damage to yourself ignoring DR & Resistance and gain the Confused condition.

66

You have somehow managed to attack one of your allies, reroll this attack against a randomly selected ally within range. If no allies are within range you inflict a Critical Injury to yourself.

67-70

This combat business is beginning to wear you out. You are Fatigued 2.

71-75

In a bizarre twist of fate, you manage to strike yourself with the attack inflicting damage normally. You are also Stunned 1.

76-78

The pain that has just flared up has got to be bad news, something, somewhere in your body has just failed. You are Weakened 1

79-80

Something twinges in your leg as you step forward into the attack. You are Injured 1 until healed.

81-85

Your attack is a complete mess and leaves you in utter disarray. You fall prone and are Injured 2 until healed.

86-90

For some unknown reason, you move 10' in a random direction. This movement Triggers Reactions and at the end of the movement you are Stunned 2.

91-92

Something gives in your upper back making life very difficult. You are Injured 2.

93

A pain shoots across your head and eyes; your head is pounding. You are Dazed 3.

94-95

Your body just wants to give up and go to sleep, the physical exertion is just too much. You are Fatigued 1 and Stunned 2.

96-97

You trip over your own feet and crack your head sharply on the floor. You are unconscious until the end of your next turn and taking 1d4 recurring bleed damage.

98-99

You miss the target with such force and strike a nearby inanimate object. You critically hit yourself.

100

Your fantastic roundhouse kick is truly amazing. Unfortunately, it does not work as you planned. All targets including yourself basic Reflex Saving throw with a DC equal to your Level DC (Hard) or take your damage and a potential critical.

CHAPTER 8 – OTHER RULES

In the enchanted forests of Everdorn, where mystical fey roamed and magic filled the air, there lived a graceful elven sorceress named Jalandria. Her ethereal beauty was matched only by her extraordinary powers, which she wielded with grace and precision. In her solitary existence, Jalandria longed for a connection that transcended the boundaries of her elven kin. Fate intervened when she crossed paths with a human wizard, the Loremaster Marco El’ zorro. Their encounter sparked a flame that burned brightly, defying the boundaries of their different worlds. As they spent more time together, their love blossomed, forming an unbreakable bond between the elven sorceress and the human wizard.Jalandria and Marco revelled in the beauty of their love, blissfully unaware of the lurking darkness that sought to tear them apart. Foul forces, envious of their union, devised a wicked scheme to separate the lovers. In a cruel twist of fate, Jalandria was abducted, ripped from Marco's embrace, and spirited away by the sinister hands of those who wished to extinguish their love.Devastated and heartbroken, Marco searched tirelessly for his lost love. Days turned into months, and months into years, but there was no trace of Jalandria. The once vibrant wizard became a mere shadow of his former self, consumed by grief and despair. His spells lost their power, and his spirit grew weary.Legends whispered of Jalandria's fate, hinting at her imprisonment in a realm beyond mortal reach. The elven sorceress had become a tragic enigma, forever lost to the world that once knew her. Marco, driven by an undying love, never ceased his quest, traversing treacherous lands and delving into forbidden depths, determined to find a way to reunite with his beloved.And so, the elven sorceress Jalandria and the human wizard Marco El’ zorro remain forever entwined in a bittersweet tale of love and loss, their souls forever yearning for the day they might be reunited once more.In Everdorn's realm, love's fire did ignite,Jalandria, sorceress, met Marco, bright.But darkness tore them asunder, love's plight,Their souls forever yearn for reunion's light.In the enchanted forests of Everdorn, where mystical fey roamed and magic filled the air, there lived a graceful elven sorceress named Jalandria.
