This chapter presents rules for a number of miscellaneous parts of the game that are vitally important for any campaign or standalone gaming session. It covers rules for the Ethics Alignment System, Movement (outside of an encounter), Falling, Perceiving, Daily Preparation, Counteraction and Afflictions.

ETHICS ALIGNMENT SYSTEM The Ethics Alignment System offers a diverse range of fifteen distinct ethical alignments. This system recognizes the multifaceted nature of morality and allows for a broader spectrum of character development and decision-making.

In the Ethics Alignment System, characters can select one of the following ethics:

Benevolence: Strives to promote kindness, empathy, and well-being for all beings, embracing the principles of good.

Justice: Upholds fairness, equality, and the rule of law, seeking to rectify injustice and protect the rights of individuals.

Harmony: Values unity, cooperation, and peaceful coexistence, fostering a sense of balance and understanding among diverse entities.

Prudence: Emphasizes wisdom, rationality, and careful decision-making, seeking to avoid unnecessary risks or harm.

Autonomy: Cherishes individual freedom, personal choices, and self-determination, allowing each being to shape their own destiny.

Altruism: Places the needs of others before oneself, prioritizing selfless acts and self-sacrifice to alleviate suffering and promote well-being.

Equilibrium: Values maintaining a harmonious balance between opposing forces and perspectives. Strives to find common ground and compromise to prevent extremes and ensure stability.

Discipline: Values structure, organization, and adherence to established rules and systems. Strives to maintain order and efficiency, believing that a structured framework is necessary for the well-being and success of individuals and societies.

Adaptability: Prioritizes flexibility and openness to change, recognizing the dynamic nature of ethical considerations. Seeks to adjust actions and decisions based on evolving circumstances to maintain harmony and fairness.

Ambition: Driven by personal success and achievement, willing to pursue goals with determination, even if it means stepping on others.

Exploitation: Seeks to manipulate and exploit others for personal gain, disregarding ethical considerations in favour of power and control.

Anarchy: Embraces chaos, disorder, and the rejection of authority, seeking to dismantle oppressive systems and structures.

Malevolence: Delights in causing harm, suffering, and chaos, revelling in the infliction of pain upon others.

Deception: Relies on lies, manipulation, and deceit to achieve personal goals, disregarding the well-being of others.

Nihilism: Rejects moral absolutes, embracing a belief in the inherent meaninglessness of existence and the absence of ethical principles.

Be aware that if you hold your ethics with unwavering dedication, you may acquire an aligned trait (see Chapter 12).

The ethics system can provide a framework for character alignment and moral decision-making. Each point represents a distinct ethical orientation that you can choose for your character, influencing your actions, beliefs, and interactions within the game world.

The chosen alignment can guide you in determining your character's motivations, moral compass, and how you interact with non-player characters and the game's narrative. It can also influence your progression, as certain choices and actions may align with or deviate from your chosen ethics.

As you navigate the setting of the campaign or story, you will encounter situations that require moral judgment and decision-making. The chosen ethics system can help you evaluate your character's stance on various moral dilemmas and determine how you will respond. This can lead to engaging role-playing opportunities, character development, and impact the overall story and gameplay experience.

LOYALTIES

In addition to your characters ethics, you may also select a number of loyalties for your character. Loyalties refer to the allegiances, commitments, or emotional bonds that you have towards another character, group, organization, or cause. Your race will offer some suggested loyalties and may include but are not restricted to

• Personal (This involves strong emotional ties between individual characters).

• Faction (You may have loyalties to specific factions, guilds, or organizations).

• National or Cultural (You have a strong sense of loyalty to your homeland, city, or cultural identity).

• Ideological (You may be dedicated to a particular ideology, religion, or belief system).

• Cause (You may be devoted to a specific cause or mission).

• Leader (You may be loyal to a charismatic or influential leader).

REWARDING ETHICS & LOYALTIES

The ethics system can provide the GM with a guideline for determining experience point XP awards based upon a character's ethical choices and actions. By aligning XP rewards with ethical decisions, the GM can reinforce the importance of moral choices and character development within the game.

When players make decisions or take actions that align with their chosen ethics, the GM can reward them with XP as a reflection of their character's growth and adherence to their moral principles. This incentivizes players to stay true to their character's alignment and actively engage with the ethical dilemmas presented in the game.

Conversely, if players deviate from their chosen ethics or act in ways that contradict their alignment, the GM can choose to withhold or reduce XP rewards. This encourages players to consider the consequences of their actions and promotes consistency in role-playing their character's moral stance.

The GM can also grant XP rewards for characters which follow and adhere to their loyalties.

MOVEMENT

Movement is something that must be tracked either for encounters, exploration or even at times in downtime. Movement during an encounter is explained in more detail in Chapter 7. In this chapter we concentrate on general movement rules.

TYPES OF MOVEMENT

Your character will always have a land speed, referred to as your Speed throughout the rules.

There are a number of different movement types available in the game, each possessing its own distinct value. Some creatures possess these movement types innately, while others can acquire them through spells, abilities (such as feats), or magical items.

Be aware that each movement type requires a specific action, with the Step action being exclusive to the Land Speed movement type.

When transitioning between movement types, you can use the Flowing Movement action (see Chapter 4) or you can simply complete one action before proceeding to the next.

Tinny Squidbottom is fleeing from the approaching orcs. He runs down the hill for 30 feet using 2 AP worth of Stride actions (his Speed is 25 feet) and then plunges into the river. Tinny has a swim speed of 20 feet and the river is 30 feet across. He attempts a Flowing Movement check using his Athletics skill and gets a success against the GM assigned DC. This allows him to continue straight into the water finishing his second AP with a 15 feet Swim (20 minus the 5 feet he had already used on his second Stride action). He then uses his third AP to swim another 15 feet across the river making it safely to the other shore.

Each speed is briefly explained below.

LAND SPEED

Most characters possess a statistic referred to as speed, which typically denotes their land speed—the rate at which they can traverse the ground using actions like Stride. Your land speed determines the distance you can cover during movement.

When a rule mentions your speed without specifying a type, it specifically pertains to your land speed.

BURROW SPEED

With a burrow speed, you possess the ability to tunnel through the ground. If you have a burrow speed, you can use the Burrow action. It's important to note that burrowing typically doesn't create a tunnel, unless the ability explicitly states otherwise. When burrowing, most creatures must hold their breath and may require tremorsense to navigate accurately.

CLIMB SPEED

Having a climb speed grants you the ability to traverse inclines and vertical surfaces effortlessly. Instead of making Climb (Climbing) checks, you automatically succeed and cover a distance up to your climb speed. However, in hazardous conditions, extremely challenging surfaces, or when crossing horizontal planes like ceilings, Climbing checks may still be necessary.

Your climb speed also provides a +4 circumstance bonus to Climbing checks. Notably, while climbing, you are not considered flat-footed.

FLY SPEED

If you have a fly speed, you have the ability to use the Arrest a Fall, Fly and Hover (Acrobatics) actions.

Additionally, if you have at least 1 rank in the Acrobatics skill, you can us the Aerial Manoeuvre action.

Flying is affected by wind conditions. Moving against the wind follows the rules of moving through difficult terrain (or formidable terrain when flying upward), while moving with the wind allows you to cover 10 feet for every 5 feet of movement spent (not cumulative when moving straight downward).

Be aware that upward and downward movement is relative to the gravity in your current location.

SWIM SPEED

When you possess a swim speed, you have the ability to smoothly navigate through water without significant hindrance. Instead of needing to make Swim (Athletics) checks, you automatically succeed and can move up to your swim speed instead of the distance listed. However, it's important to note that moving vertically, either upward or downward, still counts as moving through difficult terrain.

While you generally succeed automatically, there may be circumstances where you need to attempt swimming checks, such as in hazardous conditions or when crossing turbulent waters. Having a swim speed grants you a substantial advantage, as it provides a +4-circumstance bonus to swimming checks.

Be aware that having a swim speed does not necessarily mean you can breathe underwater. If you find yourself submerged, you may still need to hold your breath to avoid drowning, unless you have a separate means to breathe underwater.

TRAVEL SPEED

When travelling long distances the GM will need to track movement and determine how far a party can travel.

The above distances assume that the terrain is flat and clear. When moving through difficult terrain the above values are halved, and quartered when moving through formidable terrain.

Be aware that when travelling as a party it is also important to note that the character with the slowest speed determines how fast the party travel.

Some terrain types may require skill checks when travelling. If this is the case the GM will determine how often a skill check is required.

FALLING FROM HEIGHT

Over the course of an adventurer’s life, they will eventually fall off something. It may be a rope bridge, being pushed from the battlements by an invading enemy or pit trap.

Regardless of the reason, when a character falls use the following rules to determine the outcome.

FALLING

When you fall from a dangerous height (more than 5 feet) you take an amount of bludgeoning damage equal half the distance you fell when you land. It is also quite possible that you will take a critical injury from a fall.

When you land after falling, you must make a level-based Fortitude saving throw to resist injury. The DC is increased by 1 per 5 points of Hit Point damage you take from the fall.

Critical You avoid a critical injury.

Success You take a minor critical injury from your fall.

Failure You take a serious critical injury from your fall.

Fumble You take a deadly critical injury from your fall.

Blunder You make a nasty squishy sound as you splat, dying instantly.

Be aware that DR does not help you when taking fall damage.

If you take any damage from a fall, you land prone. You can Grab an Edge (Climbing) as a reaction to reduce the damage from some falls. In addition, if you fall into water, snow, or another relatively soft substance, you can treat the fall as though it were 20 feet shorter, or 30 feet shorter if you intentionally dove in. The effective reduction can’t be greater than the depth (so when falling into 10-foot-deep water, you treat the fall as 10 feet shorter).

Kaleb is pushed off the edge of a building and falls some 20 feet to the ground. As he is dressed in heavy armour he doesn’t bother making a check to stop himself from falling and simply drops like a stone. Kaleb is level (level DC 19) and has a Fortitude saving throw of +10. As he falls 20 feet, he takes 10 damage and the save DC is increased by 2. Kaleb rolls a 14 on the d20 giving him a result of 24. This is a success so he takes a Minor bludgeoning critical.

FALLING SPEED

Falling from a great height is controlled by the laws of physics and although we have no intention of reproducing such things here, we still need some mechanics to determine how quickly you fall.

You fall approximately 500 feet in the first round of any fall (or less if you hit the floor first). Each subsequent round of falling, you will drop about 1,500 feet.

Be aware that unless you make some kind of skill check, falling pretty much any distance will always use a minimum of 1 AP during an encounter.

FALLING ON A CREATURE

If you land on a creature after falling, that creature must make a DC 20 Reflex Saving Throw.

Critical The creature takes no damage.

Success The creature takes bludgeoning damage equal to one-quarter the falling damage you took.

Failure The creature takes bludgeoning damage equal to half the falling damage you took and also takes a bludgeoning critical of one degree less severity (none if the initial was minor).

Fumble The creature takes the same amount of bludgeoning damage you took from the fall and also takes a bludgeoning critical of equal severity.

FALLING OBJECTS

Falling objects take damage in the same way as characters. If dropped on a character, they use the falling on the creature rules above, although the GM may make some modifications based upon the size of the item.

PERCEIVING

Your Perception skill controls how aware you are and how easy it is for you to notice things. The two actions that are available to you when attempting to locate creatures and objects are Awareness and Search.

As a general rule, Awareness checks are made when the GM prompts you to notice something and you will make Search checks when you are actively looking for something.

There are a number of things to take into consideration when using the Perception skill such as light, visibility and other senses which allow you to locate things.

SENSES

The ways in which your character can use the Perception skill are based entirely upon the different sense that you possess. A standard humanoid creature will usually possess the senses of vision, hearing, smell, taste and touch.

Each sense belongs to a sense category and is handled in a slightly different way as described below.

PRIMARY SENSES

A primary sense can be used to detect any creatures that are not hiding or obscured to you. Using a primary sense is the only way to target a creature without drawbacks. If a target is hiding from you, you can use the Search action to locate it.

Each primary sense has a range equal to 100 + Wis x 10 in feet.

Vision is an example of a primary sense.

SECONDARY SENSES

A secondary sense is not as reliable as a primary sense when it comes to locating creatures. Any creature that you sense entirely using a secondary sense will have the hidden condition to you.

Each secondary sense has a range equal to 50 + Wis x 10 in feet.

Hearing is an example of a secondary sense.

TERTIARY SENSES

In addition to primary and secondary senses, you also possess tertiary senses. These senses assist in detecting the presence of something but struggle to pinpoint its exact location. While a tertiary sense may enable you to perceive an unnoticed creature as undetected, it provides little additional information beyond that.

Each tertiary sense has a range equal to 30 + Wis x 5 in feet.

Smell is an example of a tertiary sense.

TACTILE SENSES

Finally, you will also have tactile senses. Tactile senses allow you to feel textures, surfaces, temperatures, vibrations, and other physical properties. Tactile senses are important for various actions, such as detecting hidden objects through touch, determining the texture or quality of items, and feeling for subtle vibrations or movements. Characters with heightened tactile senses may have advantages in tasks that rely on touch, such as picking locks, identifying forgeries, or detecting concealed objects.

Each tactile sense has a range of touch.

Taste and Touch are both examples of a tactile sense.

SPECIAL SENSES

A number of creatures have senses which enable them to locate things a lot easier than a standard human. Elves and dwarves for example have excellent sight in dark areas and a wolf has a keen sense of smell which is far superior to that of most humanoids.

Special senses grant an enhanced perceptive acuity and allow creatures to potentially ignore or reduce penalties associated with sensing. All special senses (except Nightvision) have half the range of a normal sense.

Listed here are the most common special senses in the game.

DARKVISION

Darkvision is a remarkable capability that enables you to see in complete darkness without the need for any light source. Darkvision only allows for black and white vision, making it impossible to discern colours.

The level of light is considered to be two steps higher for you when using Darkvision (see below).

PERFECT DARKVISION

Perfect Darkvision works in the same way as Darkvision but enables you to see even in magical darkness in black and white and normal darkness in colour.

The level of light is considered to be three steps higher for you when using perfect Darkvision (see below).

NIGHTVISION

A creature with Nightvision has superior vision in dark areas and with a small amount of light can see pretty well. This sense has the same range as your normal vision.

The level of light is considered to be one step higher for you when using Nightvision (see below).

SCENT

Scent is the ability to detect creatures or objects through a more powerful sense of smell and is a secondary sense. This sense is effective only if the target emits a scent or aroma (incorporeal creatures, for example, usually do not emit any scent).

When a creature emits a strong scent or is upwind, the GM has the discretion to increase the range of the sense accordingly. Conversely, if a creature is downwind, the GM may choose to reduce the range of scent abilities.

BLINDSIGHT

Blindsight is an unusual sense that allows you (or a creature) to sense detect creatures using what would normally be a secondary sense such as hearing and gain the equivalent sensory information as a primary sense. Blindsight will usually have the range of a secondary sense.

An example of blindsight is the echolocation of a bat, which uses sound to locate things around it.

TREMORSENSE

Tremorsense detects the location of anything in contact with the ground and is a secondary sense. Aquatic creatures with tremorsense can also detect the location of creatures moving through water.

If you have tremorsense, you must maintain contact with the ground, while the other creatures need to be engaged in physical actions, such as casting spells with somatic components, to be detected by the creature with tremorsense. It is not necessary for the creatures to physically move from one place to another for detection to occur.

DETECTING CREATURES

Whether you can sense a creature is handled by a number of conditions. These conditions are Concealed, Hidden, Invisible, Observed, Undetected and Unnoticed. These conditions are explained in the Appendix.

LIGHT

Many creatures have a fear of the dark and you can never overlook the importance of a good light source.

The level of illumination in a particular area determines the clarity of your vision. There are ten levels of light as detailed below.

Each light source applies a modifier to the range at which your visual senses work and can also apply a penalty to visual perception checks.

• Abyssal Darkness (No Visibility): A profound and suffocating darkness that seems to devour all light. This level of darkness is infused with malevolent energy, rendering even Darkvision ineffective and creating a sense of foreboding. Within its depths, visibility is reduced to absolute zero, making navigation and perception nearly impossible.

• Supernatural Darkness (No Visibility): An otherworldly darkness that defies normal light sources, negating most forms of illumination and requiring specific abilities or magic to penetrate.

• Pitch Black (No Visibility): Complete darkness where no natural or artificial light penetrates, rendering vision impossible without specialized means such as Darkvision or light sources.

• Shadowy Darkness (20% visibility, -10 penalty) : Areas where light is scarce, enveloped in shadows that obscure details and impose significant penalties to perception checks.

• Dim Light (40% visibility, -5 penalty): Areas with reduced illumination, making it harder to see fine details and imposing a slight penalty to perception checks.

• Twilight (60% visibility, -2 penalty): The transition period between light and darkness, casting a soft glow with limited visibility and imposing moderate penalties to perception checks.

• Flickering Light (80% visibility, -1 penalty): Unsteady or intermittent light sources that cast shifting shadows, creating a sense of unease and occasional difficulty in perceiving details.

• Bright Light (100% visibility): Well-lit areas with ample illumination, offering good visibility and no penalties to perception checks.

• Radiant Light (100% visibility): Powerful illumination that bathes the area in a brilliant glow, providing clear visibility and no penalties to perception checks.

• Blinding Light: Intensely bright light that overwhelms the senses, causing temporary blindness within its radius.

By default, most areas are considered to be in bright light unless specified otherwise.

Be aware that special senses such as Darkvision cannot increase the illumination level above 8.

DAILY PREPARATION

Once every 24 hours, usually at the beginning of the day you spend an hour in preparation. To use daily preparation you must have fully rested (typically 8 hours).

There are a number of activities that you perform during your daily preparation including, but not limited to the following:

• Learned casters memorise the spells that they will able to cast for the day.

• Any abilities which have a number of uses per day are reset.

• Charged magical items regain PP (see Chapter 11).

• Spells with a duration of 24 hours or less end.

• Any other options or abilities which state that they must be refreshed during daily preparation.

COUNTERACTION

You will sometimes be required to pit two abilities together with the intention of dispelling the original effect. To do this, you must compare the respective power levels and then make a Counteract check.

COUNTERACT

Requirements You have just used an action which forces a counteract check.

Action Cost Free

Make an opposed check against the DC of the ability or effect that you are attempting to counteract. Use your Cast a Spell result or any other skill check which is appropriate to the situation. The check is modified by +/-2 for each level or PP difference between your counteract action and that of the effect you are attempting to remove.

Merrick the gnomish wizard has cast a 10 PP Mage Armour spell upon himself and feels pretty secure. Whilst exploring a dungeon with his companions. He encounters an enemy caster who immediately attempts to strip him of his defence. The enemy caster makes a Dispel (Power Manipulation) check in an attempt to counteract the Mage Armour spell and uses 8 PP. Due to the fact that this is 2 PP less than that of the Mage Armour spell, he takes a -4 penalty to the check.

EXPLORATION & DOWNTIME

When an RPG is not involved in an active encounter, the game takes on a slightly different pace with characters allowed to explore numerous options and activities.

Many of the actions which are detailed in Chapter 4 take place in a matter of minutes, hours, days or even weeks. Detailed in this section are a number of factors which must be taken into consideration when running an adventure or campaign outside of an encounter.

FOOD & WATER

Characters who refrain from consuming food or drink will endure the debilitating effects of exhaustion (as described in Chapter 7), and these effects cannot be alleviated until the character adequately replenishes themselves by consuming the required amounts of food and water.

FOOD

The amount of food that you require per day can vary depending on factors such as your race (halflings just love to eat), size, activity level, and the specific game system or setting being used. However, as a general guideline, you typically consume around 1 to 2 pounds of food per day to sustain your energy levels and maintain your physical and mental capabilities.

This food can consist of a combination of rations, fresh ingredients, and foraged or hunted food sources, depending on the availability and circumstances within the game world.

Each day that you consume less than the required amount of food (within reason), your GM will require you to make an Exhaustion check.

WATER

You typically requires around 1 gallon of water per day to maintain proper hydration and sustain your physical and performance. This amount can vary depending on factors such as your size, activity level, environmental conditions, and the game system or setting being used. It's important for you to have access to clean and drinkable water sources, whether from water skins, canteens, or natural sources like rivers or wells, to stay hydrated and avoid the detrimental effects of dehydration during their quests and adventures.

After a day with no water, your GM will require you to begin making Exhaustion checks every hour.

REST & SLEEP

You may have near superhuman abilities and spells, but you still need to replenish and rest.

REST

Rest is normally managed in 1 hour blocks and allows you to recover short term ailments, injuries, HP and PP. To rest properly, it is assumed that you take part in minimal activity and spend most of the hour relaxing.

Be aware that it is impossible to use any action with the concentrate trait whilst resting, except those available to the Meditation skill.

SLEEP

It is assumed that you will need approximately 8 hours sleep every day to maintain your physical and mental acuity. Based upon your race, these values may vary. Sleep is important to recovering HP, healing from injuries, recovering PP and generally recovering from a number of other conditions.

Each day that you are deprived of sleep you will be required to make an Exhaustion check.

FATIGUEDYou are tired, weary or otherwise lacking in physical energy. You’re fatigued value is applied as a status penalty to all actions. If your Fatigue level reaches 10 or higher, you fall unconscious until your fatigued condition is reduced and if your Fatigue level reaches 20 or higher, you die.Be aware that being unconscious from this condition does not count as rest for the purposes of recovering fatigue.FATIGUE RECOVERYAfter every hour of rest, you make a Level based Fortitude Saving Throw to recover from fatigue. Critical You reduce your fatigue level by 2Success You reduce your fatigue level by 1Fumble You increase your fatigue level by 1If you have a full nights rest you automatically reduce your fatigue value to 0. Be aware that your GM will have the final say as to whether rest and sleep will recover your fatigue level. Fatigue gained through physical or mental exertion may well be recovered, but fatigue gained through lack of food or water is unlikely to be recovered until you receive proper nourishment.FATIGUEDYou are tired, weary or otherwise lacking in physical energy. You’re fatigued value is applied as a status penalty to all actions. If your Fatigue level reaches 10 or higher, you fall unconscious until your fatigued condition is reduced and if your Fatigue level reaches 20 or higher, you die.Be aware that being unconscious from this condition does not count as rest for the purposes of recovering fatigue.FATIGUE RECOVERYAfter every hour of rest, you make a Level based Fortitude Saving Throw to recover from fatigue. Critical You reduce your fatigue level by 2Success You reduce your fatigue level by 1Fumble You increase your fatigue level by 1If you have a full nights rest you automatically reduce your fatigue value to 0. Be aware that your GM will have the final say as to whether rest and sleep will recover your fatigue level. Fatigue gained through physical or mental exertion may well be recovered, but fatigue gained through lack of food or water is unlikely to be recovered until you receive proper nourishment.

DOWNTIME ACTIVITIES

Downtime activities refer to the various tasks and endeavours that you can pursue during periods of rest and relaxation between adventures. These activities provide opportunities for you to engage in personal development, pursue personal goals, and interact with the game world in ways beyond combat and questing. Some common examples of downtime activities are explored below.

CRAFTING & ITEM CREATION

You can spend your downtime crafting new weapons, armour, magical items, or other useful equipment, utilizing your skills and resources to create valuable assets. The rules for crafting are explored in more detail in Chapter 4.

EARNING INCOME

Earning income during downtime refers to your ability to engage in activities that generate monetary rewards or resources while they are not actively adventuring. This allows you to sustain yourself financially, acquire wealth, and fund your future endeavours. The rules for earning income are explored in more detail in Chapter 4.

TRAINING & SKILL DEVELOPMENT

You can devote your time to training, honing your existing skills, or learning new ones, improving your abilities, or gaining new proficiencies and feats. Generally speaking, this kind of activity is intended to be used upon a character gaining a level or preparing for the next advancement.

Some GM’s may allow players minor gains for particularly well thought out training and development without gaining a level.

It is also possible for a character to retrain an individual skill, feat or spell during downtime. Such details are left to the discretion of the GM.

RESEARCH & STUDY

You can delve into libraries, seek out sages, or consult ancient tomes to acquire new knowledge, uncover secrets, decipher arcane texts, or gain insights into the campaign world's lore. Such things would be covered by using the Research action with specifics determined by the GM.

SOCIALISING & RELATIONSHIP BUILDING

You can engage in social activities, forge alliances, build relationships with NPCs, establish connections with influential individuals, or deepen existing bonds with party members. There are a number of social skills in Chapter 4 which can be utilised towards these ends.

REST & RECOVERY

You can use downtime to rest, recuperate, and tend to any long term injuries. How long it takes for injuries to heal naturally or be treated is explored in more detail in Chapters 4 & 7.

EXPLORATION & INFORMATION GATHERING

You can explore the campaign world's cities, wilderness, or distant lands, gathering information, uncovering rumours, discovering hidden locations, or conducting reconnaissance for future quests. There are a number of skills in Chapter 4 which can be utilised towards these ends.

ANYTHING ELSE

This downtime activities explored here are far from exhaustive. Feel free to discuss any other actions or activities that you would like to partake in with your GM.

AFFLICTIONS

Engaging in combat and triumphing over monstrous foes is one challenge, but the ominous threat of a stealthy assailant that drains your vitality silently is truly terrifying; afflictions, such as poisons, diseases, and even curses under specific conditions, pose a formidable danger.

All afflictions have a standard format when appearing as an item, spell or monster ability.

NAME & TRAITS

The initial information regarding an affliction is its name and any applicable traits. The traits will determine the type of afflictions (curse, disease, poison etc).

LEVEL

Every affliction has a level which determines how difficult it is to resist with a saving throw. For afflictions such as poisons, this will also determine the cost of the poison and how difficult it is to create. An affliction inflicted by a creature, will usually have a level that is equal to the creature.

Be aware that an affliction may be more difficult to resist if it has a rarity trait such as uncommon or rare.

SAVING THROW

Initial exposure to an affliction grants you a saving throw:

Success You are unaffected by the affliction and need not attempt any further saving throws.

Failure After the afflictions initial incubation period has passed, you progress to stage 1 and are subjected to the listed effect.

Fumble After the afflictions initial incubation period has passed, you progress to stage 2 and are subjected to the listed effect.

Be aware that some afflictions may have a different saving throw format.

INCUBATION

Every affliction has an incubation period. During this time, the target of the affliction suffers no adverse conditions. Once the incubation period has ended, the target is subjected to the appropriate stage of the affliction (based upon saving throw failure).

DURATION

An affliction will always have a duration. This determines the maximum amount of time an affliction can last if no successful saving throws are made.

STAGES

An affliction will normally have multiple stages. Each stage will list an effect and an interval (unless the interval is the same as the incubation time). When you reach an afflictions given stage, you are subjected to its effects. At the end of each stages interval, you must attempt a new saving throw.

Critical You reduce the afflictions stage by 2.

Success You reduce the afflictions stage by 1.

Failure You increase the afflictions stage by 1.

Fumble You increase the afflictions stage by 2.

If the afflictions stage is ever reduced below 1, the affliction ends. If the stage is increased beyond its maximum value, the affliction instead repeats the effects of its highest stage.

SOME EXAMPLE AFFLICTIONS

Listed here are a few example afflictions to get you started.

CONDITIONS

Any condition that you gain from an affliction lasts beyond its duration and cannot be removed while the affliction persists.
