REWARDS

In TRG, the rewards system is designed to provide a sense of progression and accomplishment for the PCs as they advance through the game. The system encompasses various types of rewards, including conviction, experience points (XP), treasure and magical items. Here's a detailed explanation of the rewards system in TRG.

CONVICTION

The TRG system can be harsh and unforgiving, and characters find themselves under constant pressure and fear of death. It is therefore unsurprising that PC’s have something that sets them apart from other characters, allowing them to perform amazing deeds even under the most difficult of circumstances. This something is called conviction.

INITIAL CONVICTION

Each character begins with 1 conviction when first created and has a maximum conviction pool of 1. At 5th level and then every 5 levels thereafter, a character’s maximum conviction pool increases by 1 (although this does not automatically grant a conviction point).

Certain abilities and feats may increase or decrease this amount. Your conviction points can never be less than 0.

USING CONVICTION

Unless otherwise noted, spending a conviction point is a free action, taking no time, and can be done at any time. You may spend only one conviction point per round. you can spend conviction for any of the following:

• Advantage You may use a conviction point to gain advantage on any one d20 saving throw, or skill check.

• Bonus You can expend 1 conviction point to enhance an attack roll, saving throw, skill check or cast a spell check. After rolling the d20 but before the outcome is revealed, you may roll a d6 and add its result to your check.

• Boost Your Defence At the start of any combat round, you may spend 1 conviction to boost your DB by 2 for 1 minute. You may only benefit from one conviction boost to defence at any time.

• Cancel Fatigue You may use a conviction point to reduce your fatigued condition by 4. Use of conviction in this way requires you to rest for 10 minutes.

• Recurring Healing You may use a conviction point to automatically succeed at a flat check to stop bleeding or recurring damage. Use of conviction in this way requires a 1 AP Concentrate action.

• Surge You may use a conviction point to reduce your stunned condition by up to 3 points.

• Other Conviction Uses As your character develops you may discover or gain other uses for conviction; these uses will be explained fully in the abilities individual descriptions.

REGAINING CONVICTION

PC’s regain expended conviction points in the following ways:

First A PC gains a conviction point each time they gain a level.

Second A PC may be awarded a point of conviction by acting in accordance with their ethics and the goals of the adventure.

Third the GM can award the PC’s conviction for a particularly impressive success or achievement in the adventure that renews confidence and faith.

Be aware that you can never have more conviction points than your maximum conviction pool.

NPC CONVICTIONSome powerful or major NPC’s and creatures may be allowed to have conviction points. The details of this is left up to the GM, but players must be aware when fighting against major NPC’s that they may pull a Conviction surprise out of their own bag of tricks.NPC CONVICTIONSome powerful or major NPC’s and creatures may be allowed to have conviction points. The details of this is left up to the GM, but players must be aware when fighting against major NPC’s that they may pull a Conviction surprise out of their own bag of tricks.

NEW FEATS

The conviction rules bring forth a collection of new feats, which are described in this section instead of Chapter 5, as they rely entirely on the Conviction mechanic. If the GM opts not to implement the Conviction rules, these feats are not necessary for core gameplay.

HERO’S FORTUNE

CONVICTION GENERAL

You have always been able to control your own fate better than others. Your maximum conviction pool increases by 1.

HERO’S RESOLVE

CONVICTION GENERAL

Prerequisites Hero’s Fortune, Level 8

You have always been able to control your own fate better than others. You regain a conviction point at the beginning of each game session.

LUCK OF HEROES

CLASS CONVICTION MARTIAL

Prerequisites Hero’s Fortune, Level 5

Whenever you spend a conviction to use the Advantage or Bonus options, there is a chance that the conviction point is not spent. Whenever you spend a conviction point, make a DC 15 flat check to avoid losing the conviction point.

EXPERIENCE POINTS (XP)

Experience points (XP) are a key aspect of TRG and are used to measure a character's growth, progress, and accumulation of knowledge and skills throughout their adventures. XP serves as a tangible representation of the challenges overcome and the accomplishments achieved by the PCs.

As discussed in earlier chapters, a PC begins at level 1 with 10,000 XP. This deviates from more traditional RPG’s where a character normally begins their career with 0 XP. Beginning with 10,000 XP indicates that the PC has already completed some level of apprenticeship and also allows the GM to begin campaigns at level 0 for younger characters.As discussed in earlier chapters, a PC begins at level 1 with 10,000 XP. This deviates from more traditional RPG’s where a character normally begins their career with 0 XP. Beginning with 10,000 XP indicates that the PC has already completed some level of apprenticeship and also allows the GM to begin campaigns at level 0 for younger characters.

PCs earn XP by successfully overcoming challenges and obstacles presented by the game's story and the GM. This can include defeating enemies in combat, solving puzzles, completing quests, achieving goals, or successfully navigating social encounters.

Here's an explanation of how XP is earned in the TRG system.

OVERCOMING CHALLENGES

When PCs encounter direct opposition, whether it's a combat encounter, peril or a social conflict, the XP earned is typically determined based on the level of challenge they successfully overcome. This means that the difficulty of the encounter or conflict, relative to the party's capabilities, is a key factor in determining the XP reward.

The XP earned from direct opposition is calculated using the encounter XP budget which is discussed earlier in this chapter.

XP awarded is distributed evenly among all members of the group, regardless of their individual contributions.

The party of four PCs from earlier who encountered the fey successfully defeat them. As a result, each PC in the group is awarded 100 XP each.

Depending upon the style of your game, your GM may wish to award XP individually and award PCs that contribute more. This can result is disparity between PCs XP and cause them to level at different times, both of which can provide interesting possibilities for advanced players.Depending upon the style of your game, your GM may wish to award XP individually and award PCs that contribute more. This can result is disparity between PCs XP and cause them to level at different times, both of which can provide interesting possibilities for advanced players.

ROLEPLAYING & CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT

TRG rewards XP for effective roleplaying and character development. This encourages players to embody their characters, engage in meaningful interactions, and contribute to the overall story. XP can be earned for well-executed roleplaying, making impactful decisions, displaying character growth, or achieving personal character goals.

DISCOVERING & EXPLORING

In exploration-focused games, XP can be earned for uncovering hidden locations, discovering secrets, or exploring uncharted territories. This incentivizes players to delve into the game world, search for hidden treasures, and uncover lore or valuable information.

COMPLETING QUESTS & OBJECTIVES

When PCs complete major quests, storylines, or significant objectives, they are often rewarded with a substantial amount of XP. These milestones mark significant accomplishments within the campaign and allow characters to progress to higher levels.

There are five levels of XP accomplishment which are detailed below:

Minor Accomplishment This level represents minor achievements or tasks that contribute to the party's progress. It could include completing a minor side quest, successfully solving a moderate puzzle, or overcoming a moderately challenging combat encounter. A minor accomplishment could be rewarded with up to 100 XP.

Moderate Accomplishment This level signifies notable achievements that significantly impact the party's journey. Examples could include completing a major story arc, defeating a powerful boss or enemy, or resolving a significant conflict diplomatically. A notable accomplishment could be rewarded with up to 200 XP.

Major Accomplishment This level denotes major milestones or feats that greatly influence the overarching narrative or the characters' development. It could involve liberating a besieged city, uncovering a hidden ancient artifact, or successfully negotiating a critical alliance. A major accomplishment could be rewarded with up to 500 XP.

Epic Accomplishment This level represents extraordinary feats of heroism or the resolution of monumental challenges. It could involve saving an entire kingdom from a catastrophic threat, unravelling a world-altering mystery, or vanquishing a legendary and powerful foe. An epic accomplishment could be rewarded with up to 800 XP.

Legendary Accomplishment This level signifies truly exceptional accomplishments that have far-reaching consequences and leave a lasting impact on the game world. It could involve fulfilling a prophetic destiny, preventing an apocalyptic event, or achieving the highest pinnacle of power and renown. A legendary accomplishment could be rewarded with up to 1,000.

GAMESMASTER AWARDS

The GM has the discretion to award XP based on exceptional player contributions, creative problem-solving, or extraordinary actions that enhance the game experience. This allows the GM to recognize outstanding player achievements that may not fall into specific gameplay mechanics.

ENDEAVOUR

The Endeavour optional rule system rewards players for achieving extreme dice rolls during gameplay. When using this optional rule, players earn rewards not only for completing quests and defeating enemies, but also for rolling exceptionally high or low results on their dice.

GAINING ENDEAVOUR

When a player rolls (or has rolled against them) an extreme dice roll, they earn endeavour which they may use in downtime to reflect upon their experiences to gain rewards.

In addition to extreme dice, a player is also rewarded for taking risks and attempting difficult challenges. If a player attempts a task that is significantly harder than their current level of skill or ability, and they succeed (even if they don't roll an extreme number), they may earn endeavour. This incentivises players to take on challenges that might be beyond their current capabilities and encourages them to think creatively and strategically to overcome obstacles.

The things that a player can gain endeavour for and how much they can earn are detailed below:

Be aware that a character can only earn one amount of endeavour from a single check.

USING ENDEAVOUR

Accumulated endeavour can be used to purchase skill ranks and feats during downtime. Your GM may require you to spend time training when using endeavour.

The amount it costs to purchase skills and feats is detailed below:

Overall, the Endeavour optional rule adds an additional layer of excitement and unpredictability to RPG gameplay, and rewards players for taking risks and achieving remarkable feats through the roll of the dice.

TREASURE

Treasure rewards come in various forms, including coins, gems, valuable items, and magical items. These treasures can be acquired by looting defeated enemies, discovering hidden caches, or as a reward for completing quests. The GM determines the value and distribution of treasure based on the campaign's balance and the level of challenge faced by the PCs.

TREASURE AWARDS

Having a proper understanding of the amount of treasure that should be rewarded to a party as they progress through the levels in a campaign is crucial. Treasure plays a significant role in balancing the abilities of the group and equipping them with additional tools to overcome challenges and encounters. Providing an inadequate amount of treasure can weaken the party, making encounters more challenging, while an excessive amount of treasure can make encounters too easy.

Thus, achieving the right balance in awarding treasure is of utmost importance. The following Treasure by Level table provides guidelines on the recommended amount of treasure to be awarded at each level, including the number and level of magic items. These guidelines assist in ensuring a well-balanced and enjoyable gameplay experience for the party as they progress in their adventures.

This table is based on the standard four person PC party.

THE ENVIRONMENT

Environmental rules in TRG refer to mechanics and guidelines that govern the impact of the game world's physical and atmospheric conditions on the PCs and their actions. These rules add depth and realism to the gameplay by simulating the effects of various environments, hazards, and weather conditions.

TERRAIN

In TRG, environmental rules for different terrain types define how the game world's physical landscapes and conditions impact the characters and their actions. These rules outline the specific effects and challenges characters may encounter when traversing and interacting with various terrains. Here's an overview of the different terrain types

ARCTIC

The arctic is a harsh and unforgiving environment characterized by freezing temperatures, treacherous icy landscapes, and howling winds. Surviving in this frigid realm requires careful preparation and resilience. Some things to consider in an arctic environment are:

EXTREME COLD

The arctic is known for its bone-chilling temperatures. Characters must make Exhaustion checks (DC determined by the GM) at regular intervals (e.g., every hour) to resist the effects of extreme cold. Failed saving throws will inflict damage (see environmental damage below).

Characters can protect themselves from extreme cold by wearing appropriate cold-weather gear, using heating spells, or finding shelter in warm locations.

BLIZZARDS

Blizzards are common in arctic regions, characterized by fierce winds, blowing snow, and reduced visibility. The GM determines when blizzards occur. During a blizzard, visibility is reduced by up to four steps depending upon its severity.

Characters caught in a blizzard may need to make saving throws or skill checks to avoid becoming disoriented, taking damage from icy gusts, or getting lost.

DANGEROUS ICE

The arctic is dotted with frozen landscapes, including icy tundra and frozen lakes. Characters must exercise caution when traversing these areas. Characters may need to make checks to determine if ice surfaces can support their weight, with failure resulting in falling through thin ice and potential consequences like cold damage, immersion in freezing water, or drowning.

DESERT

Deserts present unique challenges with scorching heat, shifting sands, and limited resources. Things to consider for deserts include dehydration, heat exhaustion, sandstorms that limit visibility and cause disorientation, as well as rules for tracking or survival in an arid environment.

HEAT EXHAUSTION

Deserts are known for scorching temperatures. Characters must make Exhaustion checks (DC determined by the GM) at regular intervals (e.g., every hour) to resist the effects of extreme heat. Failed saving throws will inflict damage (see environmental damage below).

Characters can protect themselves from extreme heat by wearing appropriate clothing, using cooling spells, or finding shade.

SANDSTORMS

Sandstorms are common in deserts and can be treacherous. The GM determines when sandstorms occur. During a sandstorm, visibility is reduced by up to four steps determined by the ferocity of the storm.

Characters caught in a sandstorm may need to make saving throws or skill checks to avoid being disoriented or taking damage from flying debris (see environmental damage below).

WATER SCARCITY

Water is scarce in the desert, making it a valuable resource. Characters must keep track of their water supplies and make Survival checks to find water sources or conserve their resources. Characters who don't have access to sufficient water must make Exhaustion checks (see chapter 7).

MOUNTAINS

Mountainous terrains are characterized by steep slopes, rugged terrain, and potential hazards like cliffs and avalanches. Here are some mechanics and guidelines to consider when dealing with mountainous environments:

DIFFICULT CLIMBING

Mountains often present steep slopes, loose rocks, and treacherous paths. Use rules for climbing, where characters need to make Athletics or Acrobatics checks to ascend or descend certain sections. Failure could result in falling, taking damage, or becoming stuck, while success allows progress or grants bonuses on further checks.

ALTITUDE EFFECTS

As characters ascend to higher elevations, the air becomes thinner, and the effects of altitude can impact their abilities. At higher elevations, characters may experience altitude effects. For every 1,000 feet climbed above a certain threshold (determined by the GM), characters must make an Exhaustion check (DC determined by altitude).

HAZARDS

Mountains can host various hazards that characters must contend with during their ascent. Mountains present potential hazards such as avalanches, rockslides, or sudden weather changes.

When such a hazard occurs, characters must make a Reflex save to avoid harm (DC determined by the hazard). On a failed saving throw, characters may take damage, be knocked prone, or become buried by debris. Successful saves result in reduced or no harm.

PLAINS

Vast and open, plains offer expansive landscapes where the horizon stretches far and wide. These regions are characterized by gently rolling hills, grassy fields, and an abundance of natural beauty. However, beneath their seemingly serene exterior, plains can present their own challenges and opportunities.

OPEN TERRAIN

Plains provide wide, open spaces with minimal obstacles or cover. Perception checks may be made to see things at a greater distance due to these open spaces.

WEATHER & TEMPERATURE

Plains can experience extreme weather conditions, including scorching heat during the day and chilling cold at night. Use the mechanics for things such as sandstorms (see desert) when dealing with extreme storms.

SWAMPS

Swamps are often portrayed as murky and treacherous landscapes, filled with stagnant water, quicksand, and dense vegetation.

DIFFICULT TERRAIN

Swamps are characterized by muddy and treacherous terrain. Movement through swamps is considered difficult terrain (see chapter 7), where characters may need to spend extra movement to navigate through thick foliage or avoid tripping on roots and branches.

POISONOUS HAZARDS

Swamps are often home to poisonous plants and creatures. Characters may encounter toxic plants, venomous snakes, or other dangerous creatures.

FOG

Swamps are known for their dense fog, reducing visibility and making it difficult to spot hazards or enemies. Visibility in a swamp can be reduced by up to four steps determined by its density.

UNDERGROUND

Beneath the surface lies a hidden world of darkness, mystery, and danger. The underground realm, whether it be deep caverns, ancient tombs, or labyrinthine dungeons, presents a distinct set of challenges for adventurers. The absence of natural light, claustrophobic passages, and lurking creatures demand resourcefulness and adaptability. Here are some environmental pointers for underground terrain in TRG:

LIGHTING

Underground environments lack natural light sources, plunging the surroundings into darkness or dim light. Characters can use torches, lanterns, or spells like Light or Continual Light to illuminate their surroundings. However, light sources might attract attention or reveal the party's presence to lurking creatures.

Consult the rules in chapter 8 to determine how much visibility a character has in such an environment.

TRAPS & HIDDEN PASSAGES

The underground is often riddled with traps and hidden passages. Characters can utilize skills like Perception and Thievery or magical abilities to disarm traps or uncover secret doors, adding an element of exploration and caution to underground encounters.

ENCLOSED SPACES

Underground environments are frequently characterized by confined spaces and narrow passages. Manoeuvring through tight spaces will often require Squeeze (Acrobatics) checks. Characters with specific abilities, such as being able to alter their size or transform into smaller creatures, might have advantages in navigating these cramped spaces.

URBAN

The hustle and bustle of urban environments present a stark contrast to the natural landscapes adventurers often encounter. City streets, crowded markets, towering buildings, and a web of social interactions define the urban landscape. Within the city's walls, new challenges and opportunities arise. Here are some environmental guidelines for urban terrain:

STREETS & ALLEYWAYS

Urban areas are often a maze of interconnected streets and alleyways. Characters may need to treat some of these areas as difficult terrain due to obstacles. Such places are often the scene of surprise encounters or ambushes. Allow PCs with urban skills to overcome some of these issues with checks.

CITY WATCH

Urban areas often have a presence of city guards or security forces. Each settlement that is encountered will have its own rules and consequences for breaking the law. There may be the possibility of random checks or inspections, or opportunities to earn the favour of influential figures within the city.

SOCIAL ENCOUNTERS & INTRIGUE

Urban environments offer rich opportunities for social interactions, negotiations, and political intrigues. Characters can engage in investigations, gather information from informants, or participate in diplomatic negotiations, with success or failure influencing the course of their urban adventures.

WOODLANDS

Woodland environments which include forests and jungles often present dense foliage, uneven terrain, and potential encounters with wildlife. Here are some mechanics and guidelines to consider when dealing with woodland environments:

DIFFICULT TERRAIN

Woodlands often have dense undergrowth, tangled vines, and uneven ground, which can impede movement. Apply rules for difficult terrain (see chapter 7), where characters may need to spend extra movement to navigate through thick foliage or avoid tripping on roots and branches.

CONCEALMENT & COVER

The abundance of trees, bushes, and foliage in woodlands provides opportunities for characters to take advantage of concealment and cover. Establish rules for partial or full cover when characters are obscured by vegetation, granting them bonuses to DB or saves against area effects.

FORAGING & HUNTING

Woodlands offer opportunities for characters to gather resources and sustain themselves. Develop rules for foraging edible plants, hunting game, or locating valuable herbs or materials. Determine the skill checks or actions required for successful foraging and the potential rewards or consequences.

WATER

Beneath the shimmering surface of vast oceans, tranquil lakes, and winding rivers lies a realm of mystery and adventure. Water environments offer unique challenges and opportunities for intrepid adventurers. Whether navigating treacherous sea currents, exploring submerged ruins, or battling aquatic creatures, the world below the waves is teeming with excitement.

UNDERWATER MOVEMENT

Water environments use specific rules for swimming and underwater movement. Characters without the appropriate abilities or equipment may have limited movement capabilities.

Please refer to Chapters 4 & 7 for rules regarding underwater movement, combat and drowning.

ENVIRONMENTAL DAMAGE

In TRG, environmental damage is harm that characters suffer due to harsh or dangerous conditions in the world around them. This is distinct from damage caused directly by enemies, traps, or personal misfortune (like falling). Instead, environmental damage results from the natural (or sometimes supernatural) hazards present in the location where the adventure takes place.

In the below table are some examples that can be used in the game.

SAVING THROWSFor many environmental hazards, an Exhaustion check is appropriate to mitigate damage. The DC should be set according to the severity of the condition and the players' level. Environmental damage can play a key role in the gameplay and story of a TRG campaign. It can add an element of realism, make the world feel more dangerous and alive, and create interesting challenges that can't be overcome by combat alone. Managing environmental damage often requires resource management, problem-solving, and careful decision-making by the players.

From a game design perspective, environmental damage also provides a useful tool to guide players towards or away from certain areas, to set the pace of the adventure, and to enhance the atmosphere and theme of the campaign. A trek through a frozen wasteland feels more real and immersive when the cold is an actual threat, not just a description.

PERILS

Deep within the labyrinthine depths of dungeons, PCs must navigate a treacherous landscape of devious traps cunningly crafted to safeguard the precious treasures hidden within. These traps are as diverse as they are deadly, ranging from intricate mechanical contraptions primed to shoot razor-sharp darts or unleash massive, crushing blocks, to intricate magic runes poised to detonate in explosive bursts of scorching flame. Each step forward requires caution and keen observation to discern the hidden triggers and mechanisms that could spell doom.

Beyond these deadly traps, intrepid PCs may encounter a multitude of other perils that lurk within the shadows of the dungeon's recesses. Nature itself poses formidable challenges, as adventurers must contend with treacherous pits, precarious cliffs, toxic gases, or venomous creatures that dwell in the darkest corners. Supernatural occurrences manifest as well, such as ghostly hauntings that unsettle the mind and disturb the ethereal fabric of reality. Ancient curses, riddles, or traps intertwined with the very essence of the dungeon's existence may test the mettle and intellect of those who dare to venture further.

Every corner turned, every door opened, and every treasure claimed carries the ever-present risk of triggering these perils. Only through unwavering vigilance, meticulous investigation, and strategic planning can PCs hope to evade or disarm the peril that lies in wait. The dungeons are a treacherous realm, requiring both courage and cunning to overcome the myriad traps and hazards that guard their secrets.

DETECTION

Every peril concealed within the depths of dungeons or lurking in the environment has an elusive trigger that sets its mechanisms or supernatural energies into motion. Traps rely on cunningly designed mechanisms such as trip wires or pressure plates, awaiting an unsuspecting adventurer's misstep. Environmental hazards or echoes, on the other hand, may stir into action merely by the proximity of those who venture too close.

As PCs cautiously approach a peril, they possess a chance to detect the trigger area or the mechanism that activates it, potentially averting disaster. By default, characters may automatically make a check to sense the presence of a peril. The check used is determined by the GM but is usually related to the type of peril that is being encountered.

This initial check allows the PCs to uncover the subtle signs or subtle cues that hint at the peril's presence, granting an opportunity to circumvent its imminent danger.

Certain perils, however, may prove more insidious, requiring a minimum level of expertise or proficiency to discern. In such cases, characters must possess a certain amount of ranks in the appropriate skill, demonstrating a mastery over their chosen craft to perceive the intricate workings or supernatural manifestations of these perils.

During exploration, as the PCs venture into the general area where a peril may lie in wait, the question arises: Do the vigilant PCs detect any lurking danger? If a peril does not specify a minimum skill rank to locate, secretly roll an appropriate detection check against the peril's Stealth DC for each PC. However, if the peril does specify a minimum skill rank, roll only if a character is actively engaged in searching, utilizing the Search (Perception) action and possesses the required skill rank or higher.

Successful checks grant awareness of the peril, allowing you to vividly describe what the astute character observes. PC becomes aware of the lurking danger, whether it be a hidden trap, a concealed environmental hazard, or an otherworldly echo. This newfound knowledge arms the PCs with valuable information, enabling them to proceed with caution or devise strategies to neutralize or bypass the imminent peril.

TRIGGERNG A PERIL

If the PCs fail to detect a peril, and the peril's trigger is an inherent part of their movement, such as stepping on a floor plate or passing through a magical sensor while walking, the peril's reaction is triggered. However, perils that require direct manipulation of the environment, such as opening a door, only use their reactions if a PC explicitly takes that action.

ACTION

Most perils possess reactions that are activated when they are triggered. In the case of simple perils, the reaction encompasses the entirety of their effect. However, for complex perils, the reaction may prompt the peril to initiate combat, rolling initiative and posing a recurring threat across multiple rounds. There are also perils that employ a triggered free action instead of a reaction, such as quicksand that can ensnare multiple creatures within a single round.

Once a complex peril has been triggered, it will follow a specific course of actions. These actions will repeat on its initiative count each turn.

RESET

Certain perils can be reset, enabling them to be triggered once more. This reset can happen automatically, such as with quicksand, where the surface settles back into its deceptive state after 24 hours. Alternatively, manual intervention may be required, as in the case of a hidden pit, where the trapdoor must be closed to conceal the pit once again.

DISABLING A PERIL

The most versatile approach to neutralizing traps is by using the Disable Device (Thievery) action, although mechanical traps can also be smashed while magical traps can usually be countered. Environmental perils can often be overcome with Nature or Survival skills, while echoes can be addressed using Occultism or Religion. The specific skill and corresponding DC required to disable a peril are indicated in its stat block, and a certain amount of skill ranks may be necessary to be able to make the attempt.

To deactivate a peril, a character must first detect it or have it pointed out to them. Deactivation attempts can be made whether the peril has been triggered or not, but some perils cease to pose a threat once their reactions have occurred, especially if they cannot be reset.

For most perils, successfully rolling the listed skill against the DC in the stat block disables it without triggering it. Additional means of deactivation and any supplementary steps needed are outlined in the peril's stat block. It's important to note that a fumble or blunder on any attempt to disable a peril triggers it, including when attempting to counteract a magical peril.

Certain perils require multiple successes for deactivation, usually due to complex components or discrete portions. In cases where perils feature complex components, a critical on a disabling check counts as two successes on a single component, whereas a result of heroic counts as three (if required).

SMASH IT

Instead of attempting to carefully disable a peril, a character may opt to smash it outright. Dealing damage to a mechanical trap or another physical peril follows the rules for damaging objects: the peril reduces the damage it takes by its Hardness. In most cases, striking the peril also triggers it, as explained in the section on Attacking a Peril below. If a peril's Hit Points are reduced to the point of it becoming broken, the peril gains this condition and can no longer be activated, though it remains repairable. If the peril's Hit Points are reduced to the point of it being destroyed, it cannot be repaired (see Chapter 6) for rules on damaging objects).

Perils have DB, applicable saving throw modifiers, Hardness, and HP listed in their stat blocks. If a peril does not include one of these statistics, it cannot be affected by anything that targets that particular statistic. Some perils may have additional immunities, as well as resistances or weaknesses.

ATTACKING A PERIL

When someone strikes a peril, particularly a mechanical trap, it usually triggers the peril unless you decide otherwise in specific cases. However, under certain circumstances, an attack that breaks the peril might prevent it from triggering. It's important to note that if a peril consists of multiple parts, breaking one part might still trigger the overall trap. On the other hand, destroying a trap in a single blow almost never triggers it. These rules also apply to most damaging spells or other effects, in addition to attacks.

REPAIRING A PERIL

You may permit a character to repair a damaged peril in order to restore its functionality. The specifics of the repair process can vary depending on the nature of the trap, and you have the discretion to determine the necessary steps. In some cases, the Repair action might be sufficient to address the damage, while in others, additional tasks such as gathering scattered components might be required. If the peril has a Reset entry, the character must follow the instructions provided there in addition to repairing the damage.

COUNTER IT

Certain magical perils can be counteracted by employing the Dispel (Power Manipulation) action and following the counteraction rules (see Chapter 8). The levels and counteract DCs of these perils are specified in their stat block. Counteracting a peril using Dispel functions similarly to making a skill check to disable a peril, following the same principles and mechanics.

PERIL AWARDSFacing perils can be just as dangerous as dealing with creatures. If PCs successfully overcome a peril, they are granted XP in same way as if they had defeated a creature of the same level. PERIL AWARDSFacing perils can be just as dangerous as dealing with creatures. If PCs successfully overcome a peril, they are granted XP in same way as if they had defeated a creature of the same level.

PERIL FORMAT

Perils are presented in a stat block format that bears resemblance to the format used for monsters. The sample stat block is accompanied by a few notes to provide guidance on understanding and interpreting the format.

THE APPENDICES

Welcome, dear reader, to the concluding section of the spellbook belonging to the renowned wizard, Marco El-Zorro - a man of insurmountable power and wisdom whose mastery of the arcane arts has become the stuff of legends. As you delve into this appendix, you are about to embark on a journey through the more obscure corners of El-Zorro's magical knowledge, where lesser-known spells, experimental incantations, and unique arcane theories await your discovery.

This appendix serves as an essential supplement to the main body of El-Zorro's spellbook. It includes extensive annotations, insightful reflections, and personal notes by the wizard himself, casting a light on the depth of his understanding and the vastness of his magical prowess. Here, you will encounter the genius behind El-Zorro's formidable power, a testament to his relentless pursuit of magical understanding and innovation.

As you navigate the detailed entries of this appendix, you shall gain a deeper appreciation for the intricacies of magical practice, and perhaps even glean a fraction of El-Zorro's own potent wisdom. Each word you read is an echo of the formidable wizard's voice, each spell a whisper of his power - beckoning you further into the realms of the arcane.

Venture forth with caution and respect, for the knowledge contained within these pages is as potent as it is enlightening. May the wisdom of Marco El-Zorro guide you in your magical endeavours, and his relentless pursuit of the arcane serve as your inspiration.

-Marco El-Zorro, Red Robed Loremaster of Freehold-

In this chapter you will find a number of miscellaneous rules and tables that can be used in TRG. Some of these items are referred to from other chapters and will be used continuously during play. At the end of this chapter, you will also find a character sheet.

APPENDIX 1 - BONUS TYPES

Bonuses can be applied to any variables or statistics within the game. As a rule you may only apply the same type of bonus to a situation once. If two bonuses of the same type are present then you will apply the higher value of the two. The term bonus can also be a penalty in most situations. If you are subject to a bonus and a penalty of the same type then they will cancel each other out. The exception to this rule is dodge bonuses which always stack with each other.

BONUS TYPES

Bonus Type

Description

Armour

An armour bonus applies to your DR and is granted by armour or by a spell or magical effect. Armour bonuses do not stack, and you may only apply the highest bonus. An armour bonus does stack with natural armour bonuses.

Circumstance

Circumstance bonuses typically involve the situation you find yourself in when attempting a check. You may only apply one circumstance bonus to any one check.

Class

You gain class bonuses from character class, feats and other sources. Class bonuses stack if gained from different sources.

Dodge

A dodge bonus improves your ability to roll with blows and adds a bonus to your DB. Dodge bonuses stack with all other bonuses to DB even other dodge bonuses. You lose any dodge bonus if you are Flat-Footed.

Item

An item bonus represents a bonus which may be applied to armour, weapons or other items of equipment. Multiple item bonuses to the same value do not stack.

Luck

A luck bonus represents good (or bad) fortune. Multiple luck bonuses to the same value do not stack. Only the highest luck bonus applies.

Natural Armour

A natural armour bonus applies to your DR. A natural armour bonus does not stack, and you may only apply the highest bonus. A natural armour bonus does stack with armour bonuses.

Race

A racial bonus comes from the culture or race that the character hails from. Racial bonuses stack if gained from different sources.

Resistance

A resistance bonus affects saving throws, providing extra protection against harm. Only the highest resistance bonus applies.

Shield

A shield bonus improves DB and is granted by a shield or by a spell or magic effect that mimics a shield. Shield bonuses stack with all other bonuses to DB except other shield bonuses.

Status

Status bonuses typically come from spells, other magical effects, or something applying a helpful, often temporary, condition to you. Once again you may only apply one status bonus to any one check.

APPENDIX 2 - CONDITIONS

As an adventurer, your journey will be replete with trials that challenge you physically, mentally, and spiritually. These challenges may result in various conditions being imposed on you or occasionally, on an item. These conditions, representing alterations to your current state, can range from fear incited by looming threats to enhancements of your speed due to a spell or a magical artifact.

Certain conditions are designed to simulate the effects of having your life essence or blood siphoned off by a creature. Others, meanwhile, represent the demeanour of other beings towards you and dictate their interactions with you.

Conditions can be transient or lasting, with some potentially enduring permanently. Many conditions carry a numerical value that signifies the degree of their severity. While some of these conditions can accumulate, others replace existing ones. The specific mechanics and implications of these numerical values vary with each condition and are thoroughly explained in their individual descriptions.

BLEEDING

Bleed represents a gradual weakening due to blood loss, pain, and general weariness. When you are suffering from Bleed you lose a certain number of HPs at the end of your turn each round in Phase 3 of the encounter turn, until the Bleed ends.

The number of HPs lost due to Bleed from different wounds is cumulative.

For example, if a character is losing 2 HPs each Round, receiving another wound Bleeding for 3 HPs will bring them to lose a total of 5 HPs each Round.

There are four severities of Bleeding, based on the total amount of HPs that you are losing each Round:

• Light Bleeding: You are losing 1 to 4 HPs each Round.

• Moderate Bleeding: You are losing 5 to 8 HPs each Round.

• Severe Bleeding: You are losing 9 to 12 HPs each Round.

• Dire: You are losing 13+ HPs each round.

If you are suffering from light bleeding, you may attempt to remove it in the same way as other recurring damage each round by making a DC 16 Flat Check. More serious bleeding must be healed with the Medicine skill or using magic.

BLINDED

You cannot see anything. You gain the flat-footed condition, and all creatures are hidden to you. All normal terrain is difficult terrain to you. You can't detect anything using vision. You automatically fumble Perception checks that require you to be able to see, and if vision is your only primary sense, all Perception checks are one difficulty level higher.

On a plus note, you are immune to visual effects. Blinded overrides dazzled.

BROKEN

Broken is a condition that affects objects. An object is broken when damage has reduced its Hit Points to 0 or less. Except for armour (see below), a broken object can't be used for its normal function, nor does it grant bonuses. If an item is reduced to a negative amount of Hit Points equal to 50% of its total, then it is destroyed.

A broken item still imposes penalties and limitations normally incurred by carrying, holding, or wearing it.

Broken armour has it DR reduced by 50% until it loses the condition.

If an effect makes an item broken automatically it is reduced to 0 HP.

CONCEALED

When you are concealed from a creature, perhaps enshrouded within a dense mist, your visibility to that creature becomes significantly reduced. Although you remain perceptible, your condition makes it more challenging for the creature to pinpoint your exact location and target you accurately. If you are struck by a creature that you are concealed from with a targeted spell or effect, you may make a DC 17 Flat Check. If the check succeeds, the attack, spell, or effect doesn't affect you.

Be aware that area effects aren't subject to this flat check.

CONFUSED

You have had your senses addled and struggle to discern friend from foe. All creatures that you are aware of are treated as enemies and you have no way of discerning between them.

You cannot use reactions, cannot use the Delay or Ready action and must use all your actions to attack any one target in range. This target must be within one Stride action (or other applicable Move action) to be considered a target. If there is more than one applicable target in range, the GM will determine randomly the target of your attack.

CONTROLLED

You are under a magical command, domination, or another form of will subversion. The entity controlling you can direct your actions, allowing them to command any of your moves, including attacks, reactions, or even choosing to Delay. Typically, the controller does not need to use their own actions to exert this control over you.

DAZED

Your mind is clouded and unfocused. Dazed always includes a value. While dazed, you take a status penalty equal to the condition value on all Intelligence-, Wisdom-, and Charisma-based rolls and DCs. This includes skill checks, will saves and any ability relying on mental acuity or presence.

DAZZLED

Your eyes are currently in a state of sensory overload. If your only primary sense is vision, all creatures and objects become concealed to you.

DEAFENED

You cannot hear anything. You automatically fumble Perception checks that require you to be able to hear. You take a –4 status penalty to Perception checks that involve sound that also rely on other senses. If you perform an action with the auditory trait, you must succeed at a DC 5 Flat Check or the action is lost; attempt the check after spending the action but before any effects are applied. On a positive note, you are immune to auditory effects.

DOOMED

A potent force has ensnared your very soul, pulling you alarmingly towards the brink of mortality. Doomed always includes a value. Your Death State is reduced by your doomed value. If your Death State is reduced to 0, you instantly die. When you die, you're no longer doomed.

Your doomed value decreases by 1 each time you get a full night's rest.

DYING

You are bleeding out or otherwise at death’s door.

While you have this condition, you are unconscious and must make a dying check at the beginning of each of your turns.

Be Aware that any time you lose the dying condition, you suffer 1 point of fatigue.

ENCUMBERED

If you are carrying more weight in lbs than your Weight Allowance (WA), you take a -1 penalty to your Dex modifiers for each 20 lb in excess.

For every 20 lbs that you are carrying in excess of your weight allowance, you also take a -5 penalty to your speed. If your speed is reduced to 0, you gain the Immobilised condition until you shed some weight.

If you are playing with a battle grid, then you always round your speed down to the nearest 5 ft.

FATIGUED

You are tired, weary or otherwise lacking in physical energy. You’re fatigued value is applied as a status penalty to all actions.

If your Fatigue level reaches 10 or higher, you fall unconscious until your fatigued condition is reduced and if your Fatigue level reaches 20 or higher, you die.

Be aware that being unconscious from this condition does not count as rest for the purposes of recovering fatigue.

FATIGUE RECOVERY

After every hour of rest, you make a Level based Fortitude Saving Throw to recover from fatigue.

Critical You reduce the condition by 2.

Success You reduce the condition by 1.

Fumble You increase the condition by 1

If you have a full nights rest you automatically reduce your fatigue value to 0.

Be aware that your GM will have the final say as to whether rest and sleep will recover your fatigue level. Fatigue gained through physical or mental exertion may well be recovered, but fatigue gained through lack of food or water is unlikely to be recovered until you receive proper nourishment.

FIXATED

An irresistible urge draws your focus to a particular subject, detaching you from the rest of your surroundings. This intense concentration imposes a status penalty of -2 on your attack and skill checks, limiting your ability to perceive other events or tasks. Any actions with the concentrate trait cannot be used, unless they are directly related to the object of your captivation (GM discretion). This condition ceases to exist if you or any of your allies are subjected to hostile actions by another creature.

FLAT-FOOTED

Your focus is diverted, or for some other reason, you find yourself unable to dedicate your complete attention to maintaining your defence. You lose any Dexterity and Dodge bonus to DB and your Dexterity bonus to Reflex Saving Throws. Furthermore, you are unable to use reactions whilst flat-footed.

FLEEING

Due to intense fear or another compelling force, you find yourself compelled to flee from the origin of this condition. During your turn, all your AP must be dedicated to escaping the source of this terrifying stimulus or, if it has a radius, to reach its outer limits. You can't Delay or Ready while fleeing. If you move outside of the area of effect of the source, you lose the condition but will automatically regain it if you move back inside for its duration.

Be Aware that you still provoke reactions when fleeing.

FRIGHTENED

Fear takes hold of you, causing you to grapple with maintaining composure as you struggle to keep your nerves in check. This condition always includes a value. You take a status penalty equal to this value to all your checks & DC’s. At the end of each of your turns, you may make a Will Saving Throw against the original DC of the fear effect with the following results:

Heroic You reduce the condition by 3.

Critical You reduce the condition by 2.

Success You reduce the condition by 1.

Fumble You increase the condition by 1.

GRABBED

You find yourself physically restrained by another creature, granting you both the flat-footed and immobilised conditions. Should you attempt a manipulate action while in this state, a successful DC 5 flat check is required, or the action is wasted. This check is performed after committing to the action but before the implementation of any subsequent effects.

HIDDEN

When you are hidden from a creature, that creature is aware of your general location but lacks the precision to pinpoint your exact position within that space. You typically become hidden by making a Hide (Stealth) check. When using the Search (Perception) action with only secondary senses to locate a creature, it remains hidden.

A creature you're hidden from is flat-footed to you. If you are struck by a creature that you are hidden from with a targeted spell or effect, you may make a DC 10 Flat check. If the check succeeds, the attack, spell, or effect doesn't affect you.

Be aware that area effects aren't subject to this flat check.

IMMOBILISED

You cannot use any action with the move trait; you gain the flat-footed condition if you don’t already have it and fail all Reflex Saving throws by 20. If an external force attempts to move you from your current position while you have this condition, it must make a check against the DC of whatever is immobilising you.

INJURED

Taking criticals in combat will often impose a penalty to you. The Injured Condition applies a penalty to all checks & DB equal to its value. The Injured Condition is cumulative, so any penalties that you sustain will build up and eventually drop you (see Injuries).

INVISIBLE

In your invisible state, you become imperceptible to the eyes of others. You're undetected to everyone. Creatures can attempt to detect you; if a creature succeeds at a Search (Perception) check against your Stealth DC, you become hidden to that creature until you make a Sneak (Stealth) action to become undetected again. If you become invisible while someone can already see you, you start out hidden to the observer (instead of undetected) until you successfully make a Sneak (Stealth) action. You can't become observed while invisible except via special abilities or magic.

PARALYZED

Your body is locked in a state of immobility, unable to move. You lose all DB except that provided by magic or armour. Furthermore, when making a Reflex Saving Throw you are always considered to have failed it by 25. You also have the flat-footed condition and can't act except to Recall Knowledge and use actions that require only the use of your mind (as determined by the GM).

PETRIFIED

You've undergone petrification, transformed into a stone statue. In this state, you're incapable of taking any actions, and your ability to perceive the world around you is completely nullified. You become an object with a weight double normal, DB 0, Hardness 8, and the same current Hit Points you had when alive. When you’re turned back into flesh, you have the same number of Hit Points you had as a statue. If the statue is destroyed, you immediately die. While petrified, your mind and body are in stasis, so you don’t age or notice the passing of time.

PRONE

You're lying on the ground. You gain the flat-footed condition and take a -2-circumstance penalty to attack checks. Any attack check against you gains a +4-circumstance bonus if the attacker is within 5 feet of you. Otherwise, they take a -4-circumstance penalty.

The only move actions you can use while you're prone are Crawl and Stand. Standing up ends the prone condition.

If you would be knocked prone while you're Climbing or Flying, you fall (see chapter 8 for the rules on falling). You can't be knocked prone when Swimming.

QUICKENED

During Phase 1 of your turn, you are granted 1 additional AP. The individual effect that renders you quickened will outline the specific actions that this bonus AP can be used for. If you become quickened from multiple sources, the extra AP you receive can be utilized for any single action permitted by any of the effects causing your quickened condition.

Be aware, because the quickened condition applies at the beginning of your turn, you will not instantly gain AP if the quickened condition is conferred upon you during your turn.

SICKENED

A sense of sickness pervades you. The sickened condition always includes a value, which translates into a status penalty of the same magnitude on all your checks and DCs.

You have the option to spend a 1 AP manipulate action to try and alleviate your discomfort by retching. This action allows you to make a Fortitude save against the DC of the effect that induced your sickness. A success will reduce your sickened value by 1, while a critical will decrease it by 2.

Be aware, that you cannot willingly ingest anything while sickened.

SLOWED

During Phase 1 of your turn, you lose AP equal to your slowed value.

Multiple occurrences of this condition do not stack, only apply the most severe at any one time.

Be aware, because the slowed condition applies at the beginning of your turn, you will not instantly lose AP if the condition is conferred upon you during your turn.

SOUL DRAIN

Upon a creature's successful extraction of your blood or life essence, your overall state of health deteriorates. Soul Drain is recorded as a damage value. This amount is applied directly to your character as Hit Point damage but also reduces your maximum hit points. If the amount of Soul Drain damage reduces your maximum hit points to less than 0, you die.

Each time you get a full night’s rest, you are healed of 5 Soul Drain damage.

Depending upon the source of your Drained condition, your misery may not end with death…

STUNNED

You find yourself in a state of stupor, incapacitated to the point where actions are beyond your reach. The Stunned Condition carries a value, denoting the amount of AP that you forfeit, each turn.

Each time you regain AP (such as at the start of your turn), reduce the number you regain by your Stunned value, then reduce your Stunned value by the number of AP you lost.

Stunned overrides Slowed. If the duration of your Stunned condition ends while you are Slowed, you count the AP lost to the Stunned Condition toward those lost to being Slowed.

So, if you were Stunned 1 and Slowed 2 at the beginning of your turn, you would lose 1 AP from Stunned and then lose only 1 additional AP by being Slowed, so you would still have 1 AP remaining to use that turn.

If the Stunned Condition forces you to lose all AP for the turn, you are also unable to use reactions for that turn.

Be aware that if you gain the Stunned Condition during your own turn, you immediately deduct the Stunned value from any remaining AP you may have.

UNCONSCIOUS

You're asleep, or you've been knocked out. You can't act. You lose all DB except that provided by magic or armour and you have the Blinded, Flat-Footed and Immobilised conditions. Upon gaining this condition, you fall prone and drop any items you are currently holding or wielding. Exceptions to this occur if the effect specifically states otherwise, or if the GM adjudicates that your current position wouldn't naturally lead to this outcome.

If you are unconscious due to being reduced to 0 or less HP from subdual damage, but not dying, you naturally return to 1 Hit Point and awaken when your HP total increases to 1 or above.

If you are unconscious due to a dying check, you must follow the dying rules in chapter 7 to determine when you regain consciousnesses.

If you're unconscious and have more than 1 HP, you wake up in one of the following ways.

• Damage inflicted to you can awaken you, given that it doesn't invoke the dying condition.

• Receiving healing, barring the natural recovery gained through rest, can rouse you from unconsciousness.

• Physical intervention such as someone shaking you awake with an Interact action can bring you to consciousness.

• Loud noises in your vicinity have a chance to awaken you, though it isn't a guarantee. At the beginning of your turn, you automatically make an Awareness (Perception) check against the DC of the noise (or against the lowest DC if there are multiple sources of noise), waking up on a successful check. If there are creatures attempting to be quiet around you, their Stealth DCs are used for this Perception check. Certain magical effects induce a deep sleep that doesn't permit this Perception check.

• In case you're merely asleep, the GM can decide that you wake up either due to having had enough rest or because something has interrupted your rest.

UNDETECTED

In a state where you are undetected by a creature, you are entirely invisible to its sight, and it remains ignorant of the space you are inhabiting. As a result, it cannot directly target you, although you remain susceptible to abilities targeting a specific area. When you are undetected against a creature, that creature becomes flat-footed to you.

If you are undetected by a creature, it can take a chance and guess your location to aim an attack at you. The creature must select a specific square and proceed with its attack attempt. This works like targeting a hidden creature (requiring a DC 10 flat check), but the flat check and attack roll are rolled in secret by the GM, who doesn't reveal whether the attack missed due to failing the flat check, failing the attack roll, or choosing the wrong square.

UNNOTICED

If you are unnoticed by a creature, that creature is completely unaware of your existence in its vicinity. Being unnoticed also means that you are undetected by the creature. This state is particularly relevant for abilities that can only be executed against targets that are entirely oblivious to your presence.

WEAKENED

You are physically debilitated. Weakened always includes a value. While weakened, you take a status penalty equal to the condition value to Strength- and Dexterity-based rolls and DCs. This includes melee attack rolls and damage rolls based on Strength, Athletics checks, Acrobatics checks, and other Strength- or Dexterity-related skill or ability checks.

YOU CANNOT MOVE!If you are subjected to a condition that’s prevents you from moving completely, then you will take penalties as described in the condition’s description. Additionally, all attacks against you gain advantage if you cannot move.YOU CANNOT MOVE!If you are subjected to a condition that’s prevents you from moving completely, then you will take penalties as described in the condition’s description. Additionally, all attacks against you gain advantage if you cannot move.

APPENDIX 3 - TRAITS

Traits are used to add additional information and detail to a specific rules’ element such as a creature, item spell or just about anything else. Some traits provide information whereas others have game mechanics which link them into specific rules and situations.

ACID

Acid effects are often corrosive and cause additional recurring damage.

ADVANTAGE

An action with this trait allows you to gain either advantage or disadvantage on the check. You may only apply one instance of this trait to any one action and if an action gains both advantage and disadvantage, they simply cancel each other out.

AIR

Air spells cannot be cast whilst underwater.

ALCHEMICAL

Alchemical items produce effects that are similar to magic. They are not classed as magical, do not produce magical auras and cannot be dispelled.

ALIGNED

There are five alignment traits; Balance, Chaos, Evil, Good and Order. Each indicates a manipulation of energies from the aligned outer plane. Some creatures will have resistances which are only overcome by a certain aligned trait.

ARCHETYPE

Archetypes are special kind of class feat. You may select an archetype feat whenever you could normally purchase a class feat. An archetype feat always has a progression requirement which must be satisfied before another archetype feat can be purchased. An individual archetype may also be a trait for a feat or ability, in which case it behaves as the Class Trait (see below).

ATTACK

An ability or action with this trait involves and attack and is subject to multiple attack penalties.

AUDITORY

The action involves and the sense of hearing. Any creature that has no sense of hearing or that has the deafened condition is immune to the effects of this action. Furthermore, you can only carry out an action with this trait if you can speak or otherwise produce the required sound.

BOMB

A bomb is an alchemical weapon which explodes inflicting damage when it hits a creature or object.

BONUS

An action with this trait compares its result to the Bonus Check Table to determine a modifier.

CANTRIP

A cantrip is a PP 0 spell which requires no PP to cast and automatically heightens in line with the caster level.

CHANCE

A chance effect alters how you roll your dice. You can never have more than a single chance effect alter a roll.

CLASS

You must be a member of the indicated class to select or use the ability. This may be a feat, item or some other ability. If multiple classes are traits for the indicated ability or feat, you only have to satisfy one of them to qualify.

COLD

Cold spells cast underwater crystalise and change their damage type to piercing.

COMPOSITION

A spell with this trait changes its spell components to those that are appropriate for the type of performance used. You can only have one spell with this trait active at any one time. If you cast a new composition spell, any ongoing effects from your previous composition spell end immediately.

CONCENTRATE

Any action with this trait requires an amount of mental focus and discipline.

CONJURED

A creature called by a conjuration spell or effect gains the conjured trait. A conjured creature can't conjure other creatures, create things of value, or cast spells that require a cost. It has the minion trait. If it tries to cast a spell of equal or higher PP than the spell that conjured it, it overpowers the conjuring magic, causing the conjured creature's spell to fail and the conjure spell to end. Otherwise, the conjured creature uses the standard abilities for a creature of its kind. When you sustain the spell that conjured the creature each round, it behaves as described in the Minion trait below.

A conjured creature can't control any spawn or other creatures generated from it, and such creatures return to their unaltered state (usually a corpse in the case of spawn) once the conjured creature is gone. If it's unclear what this state would be, the GM decides. Conjured creatures can be banished by various spells and effects. They are automatically banished if reduced to 0 Hit Points or if the spell that called them ends.

CONSUMABLE

An item with this trait is a single use item which is destroyed after its activation. When you create an item with this trait it is usually created in batches.

CONTACT

A poison with this trait is delivered when it makes contact with the skin.

CONVICTION

A conviction ability may only be used once per round. Furthermore, it may not be used in conjunction with either the chance or advantage traits.

CURSE

A curse is an effect that places a long term affliction upon a creature or a place. A curse is always magical.

DARKNESS

An effect with this trait attempts to counter any effect with the light trait.

DEFENCE

You may only use one action or ability with this trait each turn, as its complexity prevents multiple uses within the same turn.

DETECTION

Effects with this trait attempt to reveal the presence of a creature or object.

DIMENSIONAL

The effect or item creates a dimensional space. If two-dimensional spaces are placed inside each other they are both nullified.

DOWNTIME

An activity with this trait takes a day or more and can be used only during downtime.

EARTH

Earth spells cannot be cast in mid-air.

ELECTRICITY

When this spell’s effect happens underwater, the range becomes Personal and the Area becomes an explosive sphere with a 10’ radius. Everyone in the area suffers the effect, including the caster.

ELIXIR

An item with this trait is an alchemical liquid which is used by consuming it.

ENERGY

The effect has a specific energy trait. Details of how the energy traits interact is explained in chapter 6.

EMOTION

An effect with this trait alters a targets emotions in some way. Effects with this trait will also have the mental trait.

ESSENCE

Essence is the fundamental life force of the universe, a unifying energy that permeates all living beings, whether they are composed of flesh, spirit, or bone. It can be harnessed for diverse purposes, including healing, protection, necromancy, and disruption. Resistance or weakness to Essence only applies to effects that cause harm. Creatures devoid of life, such as constructs, and inanimate objects are immune to the effects of Essence.

EXPLORE

An action with this trait is can only be used when you are not in an active encounter.

FEAR

Any effect which invokes fear has this trait. Effects with this trait will also have the emotion and mental traits.

FIRE

Fire spells cannot be cast underwater. Also, any effect or item generated by a fire spell is suppressed when submerged.

FLOURISH

An action with this trait is very taxing and can only be attempted once per turn.

FOCUS

An ability with this trait can be replenished and used again if you take a Refocus (Mental Focus) action (level-based DC).

FORCE

A spell, ability, or effect that harnesses or manipulates physical or metaphysical forces. It represents the power to exert control over energy, matter, or the fundamental forces of nature.

HEALING

A healing effect restores a creature's body, typically by restoring Hit Points, but sometimes by removing diseases or other debilitating effects.

HERITAGE

A feat with this trait may only be selected at level 1.

HERB

An item with this trait is consumable and will spoil within 24 hours if unprepared. A prepared herb spoils after 1 month unless noted otherwise.

INGESTED

A poison with this trait is delivered when consumed.

INJURY

A poison with this trait is applied to a weapon and delivered by inflicting damage to the target.

INVESTED

A magical item with this trait must be invested using the Invest Item action before its abilities can be fully utilised.

LIGHT

An effect with this trait increases the illumination level in its area of effect. Any spell that has this trait increase the illumination level by one step (max 8), unless its description states otherwise.

LINGUISTIC

An effect with this trait depends on language comprehension. A linguistic effect that targets a creature works only if the target understands the language you are using.

MAGICAL

An action, effect or item with this trait is magical. If it is an attack, it overcomes magical damage reduction. This action can be sensed with the sense magic action. This trait may also be represented by one of the eight schools of magic.

MANIPULATE

You must physically manipulate an item or make gestures to use an action with this trait. Creatures without a suitable appendage can’t perform actions with this trait. Manipulate actions often trigger reactions.

MENTAL

A mental effect influences or alters the mind of the target. Objects and mindless creatures are immune to effects with this trait.

MINDLESS

A mindless creature has either programmed or rudimentary mental attributes. They take a -5 racial modifier to their Intelligence and Charisma ability scores. They are immune to all mental effects.

MINION

Minions are creatures that directly serve another creature. You can control an amount of levels of creatures with this trait at any one time equal to your Control Levels (see the Magic Chapter). Your minion acts on your turn in combat. If you spend an AP to command it will act as you bid, otherwise the minion will act according to its own alignment and motivations (see below). The action you use to command will depend upon the type of minion. For an animal companion, you Command an Animal; for a minion that’s a spell or magic item effect, like a summoned minion, you Sustain a Spell or Sustain an Activation; if not otherwise specified, you issue a verbal command, a single action with the auditory and concentrate traits.

Minion creatures who are not commanded will act based upon their alignment and motivations. Your relationship with such a creature will usually determine how this plays out. A loyal animal companion is likely to defend you whereas a summoned demon is likely to turn on you and your allies.

MORPH

Any effect which slightly amends a creature’s form has this trait. Any strikes granted by a morph effect are magical. You can benefit from multiple morph effects but if you attempt to morph the same body part more than once, the second morph attempts to counteract the first. Furthermore, a polymorph effect which alters the entire body, immediately ends a morph effect.

MOVEMENT

An action with this trait involves moving from one location to another.

OPEN

These actions work only as the first salvo on your turn. You can use an action with the open trait only if you haven't used an action with the attack or open trait yet this turn.

PENETRATING

If a spell or effect has the penetrating trait, it bypasses non-magical barriers and can counteract magical ones in an attempt to pass through them.

POISON

An effect with this trait inflicts poison damage or some kind of poison affliction. Poison damage bypasses physical resistances.

POLYMORPH

A spell or an affect with this trait is a type of magic that allows you to transform yourself (or sometimes another) into a different form or shape. The exact mechanics of how polymorph spells work can vary depending on the specific spell or ability used. When you polymorph into another form all of your equipment changes with you unless your new form can still utilise it in any way. Any merged equipment cannot be used unless it provides a static magical bonus.

Be aware that you can only benefit from one polymorph effect at any one time and any subsequent affect attempts to counter the prior.

PRESS

An action with this trait allows you to follow up earlier attacks. Actions with the press trait can be used only if you are currently affected by a multiple attack penalty.

RACE

There are many race traits and there interaction with the rules is wide and varied. Each race in the game has its own race trait, and a member of that race gains the trait. How a race trait interacts with different rules is explained in the individual rule.

RARE

Anything that has this trait is more difficult to identify, find and use. All checks in relation to the entity with this trait have their DC increased by +5. Spells with this trait cannot be selected with automatic picks and must be located during the campaign.

REVELATION

Effects with this traits reveal the true form of things or reveal hidden truths.

RITUAL

A spell that has the ritual trait is cast over a long period of time, usually an hour or greater. The GM may allow modifiers for additional casters and foci while the spell is being cast

ROD

You can only gain the benefits of one magical item with this trait each round. Furthermore, you may only use an item with the trait once per turn. You cannot combine the effects of an item with this trait with other magical items that cast spells such as scrolls, staves and wands.

RAGE

You must be in a state of rage to use abilities and actions that have this trait.

RUNE

A spell or magical effect with this trait has been created using a form of written text magic. Rune mages and certain abilities in the game will affect a spell with this trait differently.

SAVE

The action or spell requires the target to make some kind of saving throw to resist its effects.

SCHOOL

Spells are grouped into 8 different schools; Alteration, Enchantment, Insight, Invocation, Shadow, Soul, Translocation and Warding. Anything that has a school trait is magical.

SCRYING

When a spell or ability has this trait, it indicates that it grants the user the power to scry. This concept involves using magical means to gain glimpses or insights into places or beings that are not immediately accessible to the character.

SECRET

If an ability has this trait, the GM rolls the check in secret.

Some GM’s and experienced players do not like these kind of rolls. If this is the case, you should allow the player to make the roll in secret from the other players and use their acting skills to play out the result.

SLEEP

An effect with this trait causes a target to fall into a sleep or be affected by some kind of dream-like effect.

SONIC

An effect with this trait cannot be used in a vacuum.

SPLASH

When you make an attack with a weapon or spell with this trait, there is chance that creatures within the splash radius also take some damage. The following guidelines apply to attacks made with this trait.

Attack Inflicts a Critical The target and all targets in the splash radius take the weapons splash damage multiplied by the severity level (1-5) of the critical.

Attack Hits The target and all targets in the splash radius take the weapons splash damage.

Attack Misses The bomb lands off target and scatters half the distance of the original throw in a random direction. All targets within splash radius take splash damage.

Any splash damage inflicted to a target is in addition to the damage inflicted by the attack.

STAFF

A magical item with this trait holds magical spells. Only one item with the Staff trait may be invested by you at any one time.

STANCE

A stance is a specialist combat technique which may be learnt by gaining a specific feat or ability which you enter by using an action with the stance trait. Once you have entered a stance, you can leave it by entering a new stance, gaining the unconscious condition or when the encounter ends. After you use an action with the stance trait, you must wait at least one round before using another. Unless stated otherwise, a Stance requires a 1 AP Concentrate action to use.

TELEPORTATION

A spell or effect with this trait allows you to move instantaneously from one place to another. Teleportation is strenuous on the physical body and you may only use one action with this trait each turn. Furthermore, if you are the target of a teleportation effect, you must make a Spatial Awareness check to continuing acting for the rest of the turn.

If you are subject to an additional teleportation effect in a turn, it automatically fails.

TRADITION

There are four different tradition traits; arcane, divinity, ethereal and verdant. Anything with one of these traits is magical and draws its power from the tradition.

UNCOMMON

Anything that has this trait is more difficult to identify, find and use. All checks in relation to the entity with this trait have their DC increased by +2. Spells with this trait cannot be selected with automatic picks and must be located during the campaign

UTILITY

Utility spells will not work on non-willing targets, so there is no Saving Throw required for this type of spell. Since many Utility spells are beneficial, (i.e. Healing spells), a character’s aura does not usually resist beneficial magic.

VISUAL

A visual effect or ability relies on the ability to be able to see it. If a target is blind, has no sense of sight, or can see the effect for some other reason, then it is immune to its effects.

WATER

Water spells cannot be cast whilst underwater.

WORD

A spell with the word trait draws upon your native voice and releases very powerful magic. Only one word spell may be used every turn and it must be used as your opening action. After using a spell with this trait, all further spell and attack checks made during your turn suffer a -4 penalty.
